subsubtopic: MR. BEATTY-LOGGING OF MEMBERS' LONG DISTANCE TELEPHONE CALLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege affecting the rights and privileges of all members of parliament. On July 17 I wrote you expressing my concern over a newspaper report that the government had contracted with Bell Canada for a computerized device that will log the source, time, date, duration and, most important, the destination of long distance telephone calls made over the government's leased lines.
At the' time I wrote you it was unclear whether these devices could be used to log calls made from the offices of members of parliament or from the press gallery. This morning my office was able to confirm with the government telecommunications agency that long distance telephone calls made by members of parliament over the direct inter-city lines may indeed be logged. It is for that reason that I rise now to raise this question of privilege at the earliest possible opportunity.
The facts of the case are as follows. This June the Department of Communications contracted with Bell Canada for traffic data service for the 35,000 line government telephone system in the national capital region at a cost of $1.5 million. The contract is for a duration of five years, beginning last month. What the equipment does is to log calls being placed on the inter-city lines in order to provide departments with information they can use to prevent improper use of the leased lines by government employees. As I indicated earlier, it will record the source, date, duration, time and destination of calls made over the leased lines. My understanding is that such a system is already in effect in Vancouver and Edmonton, and is also being considered for other centres.
I should stress that this system does not listen in on calls in any way; what it does is to record vital information about the nature of the calls, including the telephones from which calls are placed and those to which they are placed.
The implications of this new program for our ability to discharge our responsibilities as members of parliament are serious. One of the most basic principles in a representative democracy is that citizens should be able to talk freely with their representatives about confidential mat-

July 29, 1975
Privilege-Mr. Beatty
ters, and this new computerized equipment will give the government the ability to log calls made legally and properly between a member of parliament and a citizen of this country. The installation of this equipment thus represents a substantial new encroachment upon the rights and privileges of all members of parliament.
If your Honour finds that I have a prima facie case of privilege, then I would propose to move the following motion, seconded by the hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Clark):
That this House instructs the government to program its telephone logging equipment not to record the destination of calls made from the offices of members of parliament on the government's leased inter-city telephone lines.

One of the interesting comments the minister made at that time was to the effect that one aim of Bill C-66 was to change the lifestyle of Canadians, dissuading them from using their cars for what he called luxurious travel. At the time I asked whose lifestyle would be changed by the bill. Certainly it would not force the rich to conserve energy because they can jolly well afford to continue to drive the largest cars possible, for any purpose whatsoever. Therefore no change will result in the lifestyle of the rich.
I also pointed out at the time that the government must maintain some credibility in the eyes of the electorate or the people the government governs. When the Canadian people see members of the cabinet sitting in the backs of great big limousines being driven from the Centre Block to the Confederation Building they lose confidence in respect of government credibility. This is not credibility in the eyes of the Canadian consumer.
The minister suggested last evening, in his reply to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, that people should get involved in car pools. I do not see ministers getting involved in all kinds of car pools.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I therefore move:
That Bill C-66, an Act to amend the Excise Tax Act, be amended in clause 5, as amended, by

That is the amendment I should like to see adopted. I spoke on this subject twice previously during this debate. a person of such other class of persons as the Governor in Council may by regulation prescribe,
This may or may not relate to handicapped people. I leave it to the discretion of the Chair and the House, but I ask for very careful consideration of this amendment. Mr. Chairman, I have a good deal of sympathy with what the hon. member has said. He referred to the clause which was reinserted as a result of reconciling the bill with the ways and means motion in subparagraph (g) which he recited, in paragraph (a) of Clause 5. I can give the hon. member an undertaking that I will seek out ways of achieving what he wants to achieve. I prefer to do it by regulation because of the wide variety of circumstances involved, because of the necessity of establishing the availability of transportation, and because of the necessity of establishing how we determine who is and who is not handicapped, which is difficult to do when you have a bland statement, if I may say so, in a statute, and also because of the difficulty of defining, for instance, such words as "commute conveniently" and other such language in the proposed amendment. These are difficulties which are anticipated, and the matter can be dealt with more flexibly and more to the hon. gentleman's liking, and also meet his purpose better than if it were put in the statute.
Having given him this undertaking, I gather the hon. member has the choice of either pursuing his amendment or of relying on my determination to achieve what he wants to achieve by regulation under this clause.

I am very pleased with the words of the Minister of Finance. It was precisely to enable the governor in council to define the meaning of those words that I thought they should be part of an amendment which applied to page three of the bill, which gives the governor in council the right to define the phrases "commercial or business purposes" and "physical disability". are others on the other side in whom I would not place so much trust, unfortunately. However, I do thank the minister, and perhaps any speakers who care to follow me might care to express an opinion on this matter. At present I appear to be in a "no lose" situation. I can either lose the amendment or have the minister break his given word to me.
I certainly accept the word of the minister that handicapped people will be allowed to get rebates if it is on the clear understanding that people generally known as handicapped, who have special provisions made to get to work and back, may claim a rebate. speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: May I inquire of the hon. member for Victoria whether he wishes to proceed with the debate on this amendment or seek leave of the committee to have the amendment withdrawn?

I want to make it perfectly clear that there are many variables in what the hon. member is trying to achieve. There is the definition of handicapped, there is the nature of the transportation which is eligible or not eligible for a rebate, there is the availability of substitute transportation, there is the purpose of transportation, and so on. I will attempt to incorporate all this into the regulations, if that could be achieved, to meet the requirements so far as possible, but the variety of situations is immense.
So far as possible I will try to meet the purpose of his amendment, but I think that no one can give him a guarantee. What I say as Minister of Finance binds the government, but no one can guarantee that the full blanket purpose he wants can be achieved because of the variety of situations which exists. However, I will do my best to try to reconcile the variables inherent in the situation.
In view of the promise which I believe I have from the Minister of Finance, I will accept the minister's undertaking and withdraw my amendment.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Does the hon. member have leave of the committee to withdraw the amendment he proposed?

Agreed.
Amendment (Mr. McKinnon) withdrawn.

Mr. Chairman, I regret the fact that the hon. member has withdrawn his excellent amendment. The minister has said that there might be difficulty in defining the word "handicapped". Surely that is not an argument. The Minister of National Health and Welfare and all provincial ministers can tell the Minister of Finance what the definition of "handicapped" is, and so can the Welfare Council of Canada and the people who administer the Canada Pension Plan. This reminds me of the kind of advice President Nixon received regarding the disadvantaged and black people in the United States, that is, "let us treat them with benign neglect".
We should not have had to ask the government to include something in this legislation that should be obvious. The handicapped should automatically be entitled to a

July 29, 1975
Excise Tax Act
full rebate, whether they are driving for pleasure, driving to work, or driving for any other purpose. The government wants to chisel a few cents a gallon from paraplegics and people suffering from multiple sclerosis.
If the Liberals were true Liberals they would not need to be asked for such a provision. No member of the House should have had to move such an amendment. It should have been in the legislation. But oh, the cabinet, these benign fellows, these benevolent people, will do it by order in council and will define who is handicapped and who is not handicapped, whether they are driving a car or travelling by bus. The few tens of thousands of people in this country who are handicapped should be automatically precluded from paying the tax-they should be getting the full rebate.
I have a letter from a senior official in a branch of the government of Saskatchewan. He is a full time employee, a paraplegic who drives a specially equipped car. He is driving his car in contravention of this bill. He drives to work five days a week, twice a day. He is not entitled to a rebate. That would be in contravention of this legislation. The minister says he will give an undertaking to consider the situation. That is very nice and very big of him. Big deal! He gives an undertaking to consider this. I would think he should have moved his own amendment to the legislation. This shows the inadequacy of his dummy advisers on this legislation.
I am sorry the hon. member for Victoria has withdrawn his amendment. This is so obvious that it should be part and parcel of the law, not part and parcel of the benign neglect or benign consideration or benevolence of the cabinet. I will move an amendment, Mr. Chairman. I move:
That Clause 5, as amended, be amended by adding to subclause (c) immediately after the word "purposes", the words: "or a person who is handicapped,"

Mr. Chairman, I certainly did not intend to take up more time of the House on this matter. In my opinion the House can only operate when both sides co-operate. If the Minister of Finance tells me that it would make it easier to leave it to his discretion to define exactly what a handicapped person is and what commute means, I am willing to accept his word as a gentleman and as minister of the Crown. For that reason I intend to vote against the amendment of the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre because I have confidence that the Minister of Finance will bring this in.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a very brief comment on the amendment. I intended to do so on the amendment of my colleague, the hon. member for Victoria, and I would just like the minister to add to the very generous, real, and honest undertaking he has given, a provision to the effect that it will not just be persons who are handicapped using their vehicles to travel but also those who have to be taken in vehicles. I am thinking of some of the vehicles provided by service clubs which carry handicapped people to clinics where they receive treatment. The service clubs should also be included in the list of exemptions, and I really feel that

this is what the minister has in mind, but I would not want the opportunity to go by without giving him the opportunity to confirm my understanding.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the remarks of the hon. member for Victoria, but it is not a question of accepting the minister's word. I accept the minister's word, and if he will examine my amendment again, he will find that it does not just deal with people driving to and from work. This would exclude the handicapped completely whether driving for work, pleasure, or anything else. Is this country so hard up that we have to chisel ten cents per gallon from people who are handicapped no matter how they move around? The purpose of my amendment is to prevent that. That is all we are asking, and in no way can the minister give his word or his undertaking to incorporate that in an order in council. I would not expect him to do that. He cannot give us that kind of commitment at this point in time. There is no way he can, and I would not be so bold as to ask him to do so. All I am suggesting is that this amendment covers all the handicapped. They are entitled to a full rebate no matter how they travel. That is the thrust and the purpose of my amendment.
I wish to read to the House from a letter I received as follows:
... I am writing to you to seek advice on a matter which is giving me cause for considerable concern. It relates to the recent tax increases on gasoline.
In my professional capacity ... one of my senior staff members, our Chief Record Review Officer, is a paraplegic. His only means of transportation, other than his wheel chair, is his car.
While it is quite apparent that the rest of Canadian society has to put up with the current gasoline price increases, I am wondering whether the government in Ottawa might be approached to give some kind of consideration to providing some relief to handicapped persons who rely exclusively on their vehicles for the purposes of transportation.
I appreciate full well that structuring and programming a proposal of this kind would probably create difficulties. However, in view of the fact that so many handicapped people, after rehabilitation, are able to lead relatively normal lives, I think it is a proposal which might be worthy of consideration, especially in view of the fact that most handicapped people-particularly in the category to which I have made reference-would find it virtually impossible to use a smaller vehicle.
There should be no question about agreement on this matter, even if my amendment is not worded well enough or is improperly placed in clause 5 as amended in order to accomplish the total exclusion of the handicapped from the payment of this tax, whether it is for driving to and from work, for pleasure, or for the countless times every year they have to go to clinics for physical therapy, considering the money they must spend on specially equipped cars, despite the money which service clubs raise for that purpose. It should not have to go to a cabinet meeting.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: They shouldn't even have to pay the tax.

They should not have to pay it in the first place, but they should at least be entitled to a rebate for every mile driven in a specially equipped car, and I will not accept this nonsense about the definition of handicapped. Someone who has to have a specially equipped car is obviously handicapped. There should be no question about it, and if some bureaucrat sitting up in that gallery like a crow on a fence wants to nit pick about something like that, I would fire him tomorrow. There should be no question about it. The whole damn legislation is nonsense
July 29, 1975

in the first place, and then the minister says that he will give an undertaking to consider this matter. What is there to consider? There should be no question about it from any hon. member anywhere in this House or from any person in this country.
The fact that we would even countenance legislation which would require a handicapped person to pay one cent extra per gallon, for any gallon for any purpose whatsoever, does not speak very well for this government, for this parliament, or for the kind of society in which we live. I ask this committee to accept this amendment without any further discussion. If it is not prepared to do that, I am prepared to stay here until August or September.
That is your intention.

Mr. Chairman, I had earlier proposed to support the amendment of the hon. member for Victoria. It was worthy of him and the people he represents, as it is of all of us. I am sure that all hon. members in this House have received letters such as the one which I would like to place on the record. It reads as follows:
We are having problems as my husband has emphysema and cannot get his breath; can't walk but a short distance: and is unable to get out to go to town or around anywhere. We are wanting to know if we can get in on the tax exemption of the ten cents a gallon on gas. My husband has to have oxygen in our home which can be taken along by car or truck. Please let us know as soon as possible on this matter ...
I presume that the minister will agree to include this category of person among those exempted, and I hope my colleagues will go along with me and reserve judgment on this and see just exactly what the application will be as it applies to these people. Personally I do not propose to vote on this amendment at this time in reserving this judgment.
Mr. Chairman, I was not going to speak on this amendment, but I was moved by the eloquence of my colleague, the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre.
We won't be moved by yours.

I hope the hon. member and the hon. member for Victoria will be moved to agree to support the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre.
Something else has occurred to me. The minister says that he will undertake to consider an order in council which would permit rebates to handicapped persons who must use specially designed vehicles or who must be transported to and from work. Surely one does not have to do too much checking to find out if a person is handicapped when he needs a car with special controls. Surely that would not happen if he were just pretending to be totally handicapped so that he could have the benefit of the rebate.
Surely it would not be difficult for the minister to accept an amendment which would permit those who are handicapped and who must use special vehicles, or be driven for pleasure or for work, to be excluded. They have to use those cars for their transportation. Surely it is not beyond this bureaucracy to devise that kind of system. In a country which designed the tallest freestanding building
Excise Tax Act
in the world are we saying that we are unable to deal with such a simple bureaucratic measure?
In a country which designs buildings in order to put on the magnificent exhibition of the Olympics in 1976, is its government incapable of designing a simple amendment which will permit handicapped people to be exempt from this iniquitous ten cents tax? We have accomplished the impossible. We have put up the highest stack and cleaned up air pollution.
And sent it to Parry Sound.

And we sent it to Parry Sound. That is Inco's way of solving that problem, but I am not asking the government to do anything as simple as that. I am asking it to do something even simpler. Very simply, we ought to design an amendment which will take care of that concern. Mr. Chairman, I have heard many assurances. I have heard the Minister of National Health and Welfare give assurances about the regulations governing certain types of disability under Canada Pension Plan disability provisions. We know what happens when regulations are implemented. The regulations determine if somebody qualifies. We have heard assurances given by cabinet ministers, and we have heard other ministers assure us that they will consider a matter. But, Mr. Chairman, the assurance to consider does not amount to a hill of beans.
Not to a hill of slag.

As my hon. friend says, it does not amount to a hill of slag. The only assurance we will accept is the minister's assurance, in black and white, that he will accept the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre. Alternatively, the minister can introduce his own amendment, which must be to similar effect. That is the only assurance the opposition will accept.
Sure, we know that the minister is an honourable man, but the bureaucrats determine how legislation shall be interpreted, and often they have the last word. I have seen their interpretation of Section 149(9) of the Unemployment Insurance Act concerning what constitutes an active job search. I have seen the decisions handed down with regard to disability covered by the Canadian Pension Plan. I have seen all this, and I am afraid it stinks. I cannot accept the minister's assurance, as the bureaucrats play a large role in determining the regulations.
I ask members of the Conservative opposition to my right to support the amendment. Surely the hon, member for Victoria will support us. Or, if the minister wishes to introduce his own amendment, perhaps he can consider the matter during the supper hour and then move it. Perhaps we could stand consideration of this part of the bill in order to allow the minister to bring in an amendment which will satisfy him.
I know hon. members are anxious to go on holiday, but the handicapped are equally anxious to hear the government's definitive answer. We are here to uphold their rights, and it is my responsibility, as a member of parliament, to do my best for the handicapped and to obtain a
8034

July 29, 1975
Excise Tax Act
commitment from the government not just a promise to consider.
I urge hon. members to support my colleague's amendment. Let them consider it as an opposition amendment, as the hon. member for Victoria moved a similar amendment. We would have supported it if it had been allowed to stand. We urge hon. members to vote in support of the amendment as we think that is the kind of assurance the handicapped of this country deserve.

Mr. Chairman, when I was speaking about the intent of my amendment I meant to say that the handicapped should be totally exempt from the effects of the tax and that rebates ought to be paid if they drive to work, drive for pleasure, or drive for any purpose at all, which could include driving for medical treatment, for physical therapy or anything else. As I say, they ought to be totally exempt. The effect of paragraph C of the amendment will be that it would give all handicapped people entitlement to rebate. The amendment would cover all those driving especially equipped vehicles. Certainly, hardly any except the handicapped drive such vehicles.
On second thoughts, perhaps my own amendment is deficient. Perhaps I ought to have added another subparagraph widening the definition. Possibly there ought to be amendments to other clauses in the bill. In any event, I think all hon. members understand what I, the hon. member for Victoria, and others have been trying to do. I hope the hon. member for Victoria will support this amendment which, I submit, will be of benefit to the handicapped. They ought to be eligible for a rebate of the gasoline tax, no matter for what purpose they drive.
Then why not do it properly?

Speak out, doc; I suspect this question is bothering you; if so, why not make a speech?
I should be willing to accept the minister's word, if he will give an undertaking and I do not mean an undertaking to consider, but an undertaking to act. If he will undertake that subsequent orders in council under subparagraph (g) will apply to the handicapped, no matter whether they drive their own car, whether their spouse drives, or whether any other person drives, I shall be satisfied. After all, the vehicle will be registered in the name of the handicapped person, and anybody else with a driver's licence can drive the vehicle.
If the minister will consider giving an undertaking to do this, instead of giving an undertaking to consider, I shall be happy to withdraw my amendment. But we must obtain that total undertaking from the minister, and if he gives it I will accept his word more quickly than anybody else in this committee. But I want him to give that total commitment, namely, that the order in council will provide that all handicapped shall be entitled to rebates of this tax, no matter for what purpose the vehicle is being driven and no matter who is driving the vehicle.
In Regina many of the handicapped who go to the special facilities in the Wascanna Hospital are driven there by their spouses. But anybody else can drive the car whether or not the handicapped person is in it; and, therefore I suppose the government could lose some small sums of money. That could well be, Mr. Chairman, but I

would rather take the risk that someone may try to do this, and I suggest it will happen rarely, than refuse the handicapped the right to rebate. Why should the handicapped who drive three or four times a week to the Wascanna Hospital in Regina pay ten cents per gallon more?
Proof of handicap could be supplied by the medical officer in charge of the case, who could witness or attest any kind of form which the Minister of National Revenue may devise for the purpose. The forms could also be signed by people connected with social agencies, municipal, provincial or federal. Any person connected with the medical field could attest. If that is what the minister wants, I suggest the Minister of National Revenue and his officials can design the appropriate forms to be signed by the handicapped, their families, and by medical and social agency personnel.
Surely the government is not worried because a few people may gyp it out of a few hundred dollars of tax. If the government is so worried, it can ask people to attest on any form it wishes to design. The important thing is that gasoline used by or on behalf of the handicapped should be subject to tax rebate, and there is no reason why this cannot be done.
I am certain this matter could be thoroughly covered in the regulations. I am certain that people connected with social agencies will co-operate fully with the Minister of National Revenue. Surely it is the least we can do. We have not been able to convince the government not to impose a tax on working people. We have not succeeded in that regard. Professional people may obtain a rebate, but not working people. Surely we can succeed on behalf of the handicapped.
If the minister will give a straight undertaking, not an undertaking to consider, but an undertaking to do as I suggest, I should be happy to withdraw my amendment. Unless he is prepared to do so, I think the committee ought to vote on the amendment.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I intend to move another amendment on the same lines as the one I moved yesterday.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I believe the hon. member for Peace River indicated yesterday that he has an amendment to page three. The hon. member for Rimouski told us he has an amendment to page two. Perhaps the earlier one should be taken first.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I will postpone mine.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre for pointing out that there is an earlier amendment. The hon. member for Rimouski did give the Chair notice of that amendment and we should hear him at this time.
July 29, 1975

Mr. Chairman, indeed I said yesterday that I wanted to move a subamendment to clause 5. I want to do so to enable the worker who has to use his car to go to work to be also eligible for the refund of the 10 cents tax on a gallon of a gas as the persons referred to in that clause.
Indeed, why such discrimination against a group of Canadian people who are subjected to the same laws and the same duties as other Canadians. Moreover, that tax penalizes more especially the active class of our society. The government is penalizing the workers who through their labour enable the companies and certain classes of society to increase their profits.
This week's Financial Post, dated July 26, 1975, features a list of more than a hundred of the largest companies in Canada whose sales have increased by 23 per cent in 1973-74, thus rising from $52 billion to $64 billion. However, out of that amount, only about 3 per cent represent a real increase, the remainder being the result of inflation.
Mr. Chairman, our economic policy is meant to promote constantly the increase of capital at the expense of labour and the purchasing power of our fellow citizens. Anyhow, in this context, the rich gather billions in net profits thus reducing the purchasing power of our fellow citizens.
And those who suffer most from it are low income earners and the citizens who do not have a decent or appropriate purchasing power. The pretences advanced by the government are at best doubtful when they say that the tax is imposed to conserve gas and establish uniform prices throughout Canada. First, nothing proves there will be economy in that field. They also claim to establish a unique gas price by taxing one part of the population to the prejudice of the other part. In fact, this other part of our society is the poorer, the worse off. The government seems to be doing backward socialism. At least, they are doing so in the present case. They penalize the poor to give to the wealthy. Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Beaudoin):
That clause 5 be amended by adding, after subclause (g) subclause (h) which would read as follows:
Paragraph (h) would read as follows: a worker who must absolutely travel a minimum of twenty-five (25) miles a week in his own car to reach his place of employment.
I rise to support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Rimouski. I presume it has been accepted as being in order.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Chair does have some reservations about the amendment inasmuch as it appears similar to that moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. However, the hon. member for Rimouski did point out that he was seeking to make a subamendment thereto, and for that reason the Chair will allow it to be debated and disposed of by the Committee.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I appreciate your ruling as, I am sure, do my hon. friends. I rise to support this amendment. While it is similar to the amendment moved by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre, it allows for an element of choice. A worker who
Excise Tax Act
had no suitable alternative transportation available to him would be eligible for the rebate in certain circumstances.
As all of us know, of course, there are hundreds of thousands of workers for whom no choice is possible. They are bound to use their cars to go to work until such time as society provides an alternative means of transportation. Administration is simplified by the provision that only those who must drive 25 miles a week to work will qualify. In other words, those who drive fewer than 25 miles a week can walk or, possibly, ride a bicycle.
The minister, in making regulations, can require the employer concerned to attest to the number of days a week, or months a year, in which the employee drove his vehicle to work. After all, the employer has a record of the number of days upon which the employee attended. The employer or his representative, say a foreman or an accountant, whether it be a big corporation or a company with only two or three employees, can append his signature and attest to the application for a rebate. There is no problem about that. I am sure that the advisers to the minister could find additional words to put in the regulations to provide that any employer who makes a fraudulent attestation will be in real trouble, along with the employee.
Workers from a rural area who have to drive ten or 15 miles to work and who have no alternative mode of transportation surely present no danger, and can hardly be said to be defrauding the Government of Canada of the ten cents a gallon tax. The amendment moved by my hon. friend providing a minimum of 25 miles per week is much easier for the Minister of Finance to accept than was the one moved by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre. If I may be so bold, I say it is probably a wiser amendment in terms of administration and in terms of applying it to people all across the country-I say that while my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre is out of the chamber for a few moments.
While this amendment does not go as far as the previous one, I submit it is much easier to accept in the context of the philosophy of the minister regarding what he is trying to do in this bill, which is first to raise money, and secondly to exempt certain categories of workers. This amendment relates to a category of worker who may inadvertently have been overlooked but who nevertheless has no alternative but to drive at least 25 miles a week to work.
People in the city of Regina who live less than two and a half miles from their place of employment and make ten trips to and from work a week will not be eligible for a rebate under the terms of this amendment, which shows how reasonable it is. If a person living in Lakeview, the part of Regina where I live, is employed on Broad Street or Winnipeg Street in the eastern part of the city, he is only two to two and a quarter miles from his place of work, and if he goes to work five days a week and does not work overtime or extra days he will not be eligible for a rebate. On the other hand, a person who lives in Albert Park in Regina and is employed at the Interprovincial Steel plant or several other related industries a mile or more north of the city limits, will have to drive 14 to 20 miles a day to

and from work. Such a person would be eligible for a rebate because he has no alternative mode of transportation.
In the case of a car pool, surely a person who is using his car and who is hauling three of four fellow employees to work should be entitled to a rebate. He is contributing to one of thd objectives outlined in the bill by the minister, that of conserving energy and making people use an alternative mode of transportation. This amendment is so reasonable that if I were on the government side of the House I would have to vote for it, even though it was moved by a member on the opposition side. Half, or probably more than half of our working people who drive less than 25 miles a week to work are excluded from the provisions of the amendment.
I do not doubt for a moment that in most medium and small sized cities, towns, and villages across Canada the majority of workers would live less than two and half miles from their place of employment, and as such they would not qualify for a rebate. The minister could also provide in the regulations that in the case of a minimum rebate of $10 there would be a two or three month wait before application could be made for a rebate. If I recall the earlier debate on the bill, they could only apply twice a year in any event, so this would present no large additional amount of paper work on the part of the Department of National Revenue. It also occurs to me that this kind of application for a rebate, including applications from the handicapped, should require the applicant to make an attestation and to provide any evidence required for the purpose of obtaining a rebate. I ask the committee to accept what is a good amendment, one that would allow a limited opportunity to working people to apply for a rebate.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to speak to this amendment. May I first of all point out that I am not in favour of this ten cents gasoline tax.
In applying this amendment I find it difficult to see how any department or bureaucrat could interpret it, either strictly or benevolently. This reference to "a worker who is a worker" reminds me of the Biblical phrase "who is my neighbour?" It is difficult to define. Throughout the debate on this bill there has been an implied or inferential differentiation between a businessman, a professional, and a worker. I think it has already been said that businessmen and professionals are workers who sometimes put in longer hours than the so-called workers. I am concerned that even a professional man or a businessman, or whatever the case is, be entitled to a rebate only when the gas he uses is for commercial purposes. I suggest that whether it be a professional person, a businessman, or a worker going to and from his place of employment, the same situation applies. I wonder whether my interpretation under the Excise Tax Act is correct or not. Perhaps the Minister of Finance would respond before I proceed any further.

Mr. Chairman, I am happy to support the amendment motion of my good friend, the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard). First of all, 25 miles a week is not a high mileage, and second, if the government accept-

ed this minimum of 25 miles a week, for all practical purposes the tax of 10 cents a gallon would no longer exist. The tax would no longer exist because I believe that if the government accepts this amendment, it will also avoid a lot of headaches for the Minister of Finance and the technocrats who have to collect these 10 cents a gallon.
Most of those who are owners or chairmen of companies are exempt from the tax and can claim the 10 cents a gallon rebate at the end of the year. These same owners often own a farm or have other employment apart from owning the companies. I would like the Minister of Finance to tell the House how the technocrat or the one who will have to decide what percentage of the yearly mileage will be eligible for the rebate will determine how many gallons will be subject to a reimbursement of the 10 cents a gallon tax at the end of the year, and it will have to be specified that the technocrat will determine what percentage of use of the vehicle was for company purposes and which percentage was for the worker or any owner of a company to get to work. There is nothing extraordinary about owning a company. It costs about $300. Any worker with a good job who makes $12,000 or $15,000 a year can own a company.
Several members of the House of Commons own companies. Several senators also own companies. These companies have vehicles registered in the name of the company. Are these vehicles used by the member? I would like to give an example to illustrate my point. If the company owns a 1975 Chevrolet registered in the name of the company, for instance, and the member of parliament owns a 1975 Oldsmobile to travel to Ottawa and takes the Chevrolet with the credit card of the company to travel to Ottawa, it means that this hon. member will not pay the 10 cents a gallon to drive to Ottawa, because he uses a company car. He leaves the Oldsmobile to the company for the week, or month. I say this amendment gives a chance to whoever must solve the problem, because I feel that act will be almost inapplicable, perhaps in fact but not legally.
I feel that from the legal point of view, there will be many pitfalls which will give many a headache to the Minister of Finance who is of good faith and who wants, precisely, through his bill, to save oil by forcing one class of society, that of the small worker, to use public transports. That may save money also for parking lots and other things over the long term. In a way, I agree with him. However, how is he going to apply the act? That is the problem. There is another bill which will be put through the mill again next year with several amendments. It would be better to amend it now to clarify the situation and pass the bill as soon as possible so we can then leave for holidays. That is why I feel the situation must be cleared up right away, so that we can leave for our holidays this evening or tomorrow. We must make it clear, Mr. Chairman, otherwise we shall never get through. In all modesty, I am the owner of two companies, one of them possesses a vehicle. Which vehicle shall I drive to go to Ottawa? The one which is registered in the company's name or my own? Which one?
And most senators are in the same situation. Several members have farms or companies in their names, even big oil companies, and have seven, eight or ten vehicles in their backyards. I recently visited one which owns six or

seven vehicles. The company is very prosperous. The hon. member can choose between six or seven cars to drive to Ottawa. He will get back his 19 cents a mile, and the 10 cents as well, if he drives the car which is registered under the name of the company, and uses the company's credit cards. What are they going to do to collect all that? How will the Minister of Finance decide and how will be officials of his department decide? This is the problem and this is why I would like the amendment, which practically aims at cutting off the 10 cents tax a gallon for certain people, particularly working people, to be adopted.

Mr. Chairman, as you have pointed out, this amendment is similar to the one I moved last evening which was defeated a little while ago. However, there is a difference. My amendment sought to extend the right to rebates to workers generally who use their cars to get to and from their places of employment, whereas this amendment would make the rebates apply only in cases of workers who travel at least 25 miles a week. It seems to me that if members were not willing to accept the other one they might consider this one, which is a little less but at least a move in the right direction.
However, the main reason I rise for a minute or two is that since the defeat of my earlier amendment, we have had a discussion on the question of an exemption for handicapped persons. May I say that it was both welcome and interesting to note that the minister seemed to have relented a bit from the stern position he took earlier. He indicated that in that case he was prepared to consider doing something by order in council.
I wonder if this softening of his thinking has carried over into the case of the workers. Is he prepared to accept any kind of amendment or proposal that would give the exemption to workers in certain cases and, if so, is he prepared to do that by accepting some form of an amendment to the bill, or is he prepared to give the kind of undertaking he gave earlier to the hon. member for Victoria and others in the House, namely, that he will look at the whole question of this tax as it applies to workers?
The minister must realize that, apart from the fact that we are against the bill as a whole, this is the feature of it which has been most offensive, namely, the non-recognition of the money workers have to spend on getting to and from work. I put the question to the minister again: Has he softened his position at all, and is he prepared to look at this thing, perhaps not with the same kind of commitment I think he gave regarding the handicapped, but at least with some sympathy for the problem faced by those workers who have no choice but to use their automobiles to get to and from their places of employment?

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I think I was the thirty-third speaker from our party to speak on this legislation on second reading, and hopefully our message has got through to the minister. The message we receive from the government is that gasoline is worth more than Canadians have been paying for it, and that wine will cost less because it has been too expensive. The government is telling the Canadian taxpayers that they should remain at home, use less gas and drink more wine. In other words, the Liberal message is: do not complain about paying the dime, you will get used to it over a period of time, and if you can't afford to drive your flivver stay at home and become a wine bibber.
I received a letter from a constituent which I should like to place on record. It states in part:
But, now let me explain why I'm really writing this letter. When I heard that the tax on a bottle of wine went down six cents I nearly exploded from anger! To think a government is so ridiculous as to do such a stupid thing makes me rage ... I plead with you to do all you can to stop this foolish business!
In the absence of the hon. member for Vegreville I wish to move an amendment on his behalf and say a few words in support of it. The hon. member for Vegreville merely wants to know whether or not the Minister of Finance will make a commitment in this House to alleviate some of the resultant problems of the tax which have been explained by hon. members.
Even though the minister states that the industrial construction industry uses gas eligible for refund he must by now have commenced to realize the importance of the point we have been trying to make in respect of the unnecessary additional cost of financing to bulk dealers, fishermen, farmers, large trucking operations and others. Housing contractors too will require extra funds, the carrying charges of which will be borne by the payee, the Canadian consumer, who ultimately will be the permanent loser. In many cases federal and provincial governments' revenue will be affected, particularly in the building of roads and highways. If this bill is not altered there will not only be high administrative costs but higher pay-outs to various road construction firms.
There is absolutely no way anyone could make a fair assessment of what the actual cash layout will be under this ludicrous and useless legislation. It is frustrating enough to have "no" automatically voiced by the government daily to every Standing Order 43 motion presented to this House, but now the same tune is being picked up by government members en masse when logical amendments, beneficial to Canada and Canadians, are proposed by members on this side of the House. Backbenchers should consider the effect such a measure will have on their constituents instead of blindly nodding their heads in silence, or speaking without any sound basis to support

Madam Chairman, I not only have received representations from the hon. member for Red Deer and his colleague, the hon. member for Vegreville, on whose behalf he presents a motion, but also from my colleagues from Assiniboia and Battleford-Kindersley. Last week in the course of debate on this bill representations were received from these four members in particular, and other members, that the bill be amended to provide an exemption for bulk purchasers of gasoline and also for users of marked gasoline, which is what is referred to in the amendment.
At that time I pointed out that there were some fundamental problems in tying the federal taxing statute to provincial legislation since this could be tantamount to a delegation of the taxing authority of parliament to provincial legislatures. I was worried about having a lack of uniformity in the application of the general tax across the country. I did undertake, however, that I was prepared to look for ways to streamline the operation of the bill.
In this context the government is prepared to amend Bill C-66 in such a way as to provide legislative authority to exempt certain purchasers of gasoline where this is administratively feasible. I must emphasize, however, that it is not certain that it will, indeed, prove to be feasible to provide an exemption in all of those instances suggested by the hon. member. To this end, if the hon. gentleman would be willing to withdraw his amendment, I think I have an amendment which would do the trick. Madam Chairman, I should like to move an amendment on Clause 5. As far as we are concerned, hon. members to my left, who are prolific in ideas, may have other amendments to move. I simply want to say that I stated to the committee yesterday that I would be moving another amendment along the same lines as the one I moved yesterday to another part of the bill. I will not repeat the arguments I made then. They are obviously unattractive to the minister. But I think that the kind of discussion we had today in respect of the amendment offered by the hon. member for Victoria indicates the need to have some form of control by the House over regulations passed by the government.
The true purpose of taxation should be to take from each according to his ability to pay. If I added to that "give to each according to his need" it might be a motto well recognized by other sections of the committee. The hon. member for Nickel Belt, who is more familiar with the subject than I am, says I am correct. However, what the government is asking us to do is to give them a license to plunder. That is the kind of system under which taxation is imposed today. Accompanied with that license to plunder is the freedom to change, add to and subtract from the plundering without any opportunity for parliament to pass judgment on what is being done. Some day this parliament will be told by the people of Canada, who I think are getting fed up to the teeth with this sort of fiscal arrangement, that they will put a short rein, not only upon
July 29, 1975

this government but upon any government, whether it is Conservative, Liberal or, what is even more unlikely but nevertheless more necessary in that case, a socialist government. My friend here says we have a Liberal and a socialist government, the front end is Liberal and the rear end is socialist.
What we have now is a situation in which the governor in council, at the instigation of the minister who has been prodded by his officials-it may not be this minister but some one else-may set an arbitrary, artificial, capricious,-and politically motivated frivolous-I have other adjectives but I stop there, the minister knows what I mean-order in council to establish the restrictions on or additions to the kind of people who will be eligible for rebates. For example, under this legislation, particularly Clause 5 which purports to amend section 47 of the Excise Tax Act, we find the phrase "a person for commercial or business purposes". In the name of heaven we all know what that means. The minister knows what it means, the officials should know what it means, and even my friends to the left should know what it means. These words have connotations and understandings which, over many years, have become fixed in our life, and for the government to say they want the right to put an artificially twisted and contorted interpretation on what "commercial or business purposes" means so they can make the rules as they see fit from time to time, is not attractive to me.
Under those circumstances, I have no alternative but to move the following amendment:
That Clause 5 of Bill C-66, an act to amend the Excise Tax Act be amended in Clause 5
(a)	By striking out line 12 on page 3 thereof and substituting
therefor the following:
"Regulation subject to negative resolution of the House of Commons"
(b)	By striking out line 21 on page 3 thereof and substituting
therefor the following:
"In Council may by regulation determine subject to negative resolution of the House of Commons"
If I had time, I might have added a third amendment which would have covered the amendment which the minister just brought in and which gives power to the governor in council to act by regulation, but I will not do that.
I will simply conclude with these words, that I do not think we should sit idly by and allow the government to do all these things, to make these changes, without some means of bringing back to the House an opportunity to pass judgment on what they have done. The dilemma of the hon. member for Victoria makes this quite plain. The hon. member says he takes the word of the minister, and this party agreed with him. We did not vote for the amendment of the hon. member for Regina Lake Centre. But that should not be required. There should be an understanding that any hon. member should not have to rely on an undertaking by the minister. There should be a proper procedure by which orders in council come back to the House, and an opportunity given to the House to pass judgment on them when the occasion arises. It is in that sense that I move the amendment.

Madam Chairman, not only do I wish to support the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Peace River, I want to commend him for his persistence. I urge him to keep at it, even if it takes 20 or 25 years to win his point. I realize that there is a general desire to get out of here, but when an important issue like this is raised, I do not think it is good enough for the Minister of Finance simply to rise and say that we have had this dialogue before.
I think the point is well put. It is introduced in a different context than when we had it previously, and I suggest that the hon. member for Peace River is being quite reasonable in proposing that certain orders in council, as indicated on page 3 of the bill, be subject to a negative resolution of the House of Commons.
I will say again as I said yesterday-and like the Minister of Finance I am not unwilling to say it over again, but of course it is because I am saying what is right-that if the hon. member for Peace River were proposing an affirmative resolution, that could be a delaying process. It could make it pretty difficult for the government to govern. That is not what the hon. member for Peace River is asking. He is asking that when orders in council have been proclaimed for the purposes set out on page 3 of the bill, they be permitted to come into effect, but that it be possible for a member in the House of Commons, within the rules, to put down a motion calling for those orders to be nullified. Only if such a motion is carried are those orders nullified, and in the circumstances of this parliament in particular where there is an overwhelming majority, the chances of that happening are very slim.
I will make the point again which I made yesterday, that this sort of thing can have a salutary effect. I think that when a minister is getting an order in council, especially in the tax field, he should have to ask himself whether it is going to get by, or whether it will result in members of the House putting down negative resolutions. That sort of questioning which he should engage in would surely encourage a minister to bring in the kind of orders in council which would be accepted.
As I say, a few years ago this was a relatively new idea. The hon. member for Peace River made headway when he got the Minister of Finance in one of his previous incarnations to bring in a bill which provides for affirmative and negative resolutions, but now the problem is to get them to be used when an actual situation arises, and I think this is a good place to put the practice into effect. I support very strongly the proposal of the hon. member for Peace River.

Madam Chairman, I am rising to propose an amendment to Clause 8. We find it to be necessary following the determination of government members to beat back all reasonable amendments which have been proposed by the official opposition, by members of the New Democratic Party, and by members of the Social Credit Party. I am thinking in particular of the amendment supported by everyone on this side of the House which would have given a rebate to ordinary working Canadians driving to and from their places of work, which the Liberals saw in their infinite wisdom to be the kind of amendment they could not, of course, accept, and therefore defeated. I am also thinking of the amendments which were proposed here today by all three opposition parties with particular reference to the handicapped.
I therefore move:
That clause 8 be amended in line 1 on page 5 by deleting the words "ten cents" and by substituting therefor the words "one cent".

The logic of this amendment should be inescapable, even to the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, who has frequent difficulty in following logic from point A to point B, let alone going from point A to point B. I am sure that even that hon. member can understand the logic of this amendment, and if she really concentrates with all her ability she could probably cope with it.
The point of my amendment is that by reducing the tax from ten cents to one cent we will simultaneously reduce the degree of injustice inflicted upon Canadians by some 90 per cent. If the amendment were passed, we acknowledge that the minister would have to raise the money to pay for the increase in the price of oil imported off the east coast by some other means. He could adopt any one of the suggestions made. He could levy a special income tax on upper income Canadians or a special tax on the petroleum industry. Probably the best way would be to take it out of general revenue. This would mean that the people who pay personal income tax on a progressive basis, as well as the corporations, would contribute the money to pay for these additional costs.
Any of these possibilities would be preferable to the government's decision to levy a flat ten cent per gallon excise tax on all Canadians who drive automobiles, 95 per cent of whom drive to and from work because there is no alternative. If the Minister of Finance had been prepared to include one of the election promises in the budget, and had proposed to do something about urban transit systems, we might have been more favourably disposed to his rhetoric about changing lifestyles. The only change possible will be that which comes from the increased financial burden on average and low income Canadians who have less disposable income to spend on the other aspects of life.
Even at this late stage, I urge that some modicum of sense impinge itself upon the consciousness of the Liberal Party. I have no hope for the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, but I have a little for some of the others. It might get through to them at this late stage in the debate that they have an obligation to do something on behalf of low income Canadians instead of doing something to them.

Madam Chairman, here we are again. This party is trying to be very helpful by making proposals to the government. We have again put forward a constructive amendment which would eliminate much of the breaking up of society into little groups by the government and then taxing them. This amendment proposes to tax everyone one cent per gallon, and this of course would be applied universally. There would be none of this bureaucratic action in separating groups and making it possible for the minister by order in council to decide who is handicapped and who is not. It will not be left to the whim of bureaucrats to decide taxation, since they have not been elected by the people of Canada. It seems to me this is the most honest and equitable way for the government to go about raising the funds that they say are required.
I recall the minister saying last evening about one of our other constructive amendments that the idea was to get
July 29, 1975

people to change their lifestyle. As I pointed out, with the ten cents per gallon excise tax the lifestyle of the poor would certainly change; they could sit home and drink wine. The lifestyle of the rich would not be changed by introducing this amendment to reduce the excise tax to one cent per gallon, but the effect of the tax would not fall so heavily on the workers.
We have pointed out time and again the impact of this ten cents per gallon tax. It places a very difficult burden on those people who live in Nickel Belt where everyone has to drive a considerable distance to work. The minister said last night:
But, to give a deduction of the expense of getting to work would be to give a tax subsidy to those who choose to drive rather than take public transit-to those who choose to live far from their place of work, rather than close, and to those who choose to drive a large automobile rather than to those who drive a small one.
People do not choose to live far from their work. In my riding, people would rather live close to work but as a penalty for building a home where they can afford it this government places an extra burden on them. This tax will take a big chunk out of their budgets and will be an extra hardship on many with families to raise. We are faced with the juggernaut of power on the government benches. We have put up a fight against the ten cent tax and got nowhere. We have tried to talk reason and have proposed constructive amendments, but are obviously not getting anywhere so, since we abhor this kind of tax we propose an amendment to reduce it from ten cents per gallon to one cent per gallon. At least the wealthy would be able to pay that tax and it would not be such a burden on the poor.
Members tend to think of their own ridings and I think of mine. In the last election the Liberal candidate was promising to remove the railway tracks from Sudbury and the Liberal candidate in my riding was saying "I want the railway tracks in Nickel Belt". The public transit system we were promised would have alleviated the problem, but people in areas like mine do not have it. The ten cents tax would be a great burden, so our proposal to amend it to one cent is a reasonable way of raising the money the government says it needs. We have proposed alternate ways of getting the money and have suggested economies the cabinet might adopt by changing their driving habits. We have suggested they pool their limousines and drive smaller cars. We have suggested economies which could be implemented by the government as an example to the working people. It is only when the government shows that they are prepared to economize that they can say to the people "Don't do as we tell you, do as we do-look how we are running the country on your behalf".
The way we are squandering the resources of this country cries out to heaven for some recognition. When we look for leadership, we look to the people who were elected to govern and say "That is an example I can follow". I suggest the ministers pool their cars and possibly use Volkswagens. Surely an across the board tax of one cent a gallon will not affect the economy drastically. You see, we are caught in a terrible game. The workers of my area will pay ten cents a gallon more, and will ask their employers for more wages. They will say, "This tax is eating into the family's budget; you must compensate us for it." They will try to bargain, and a strike may or may not follow. If there
Excise Tax Act
is no strike, it means that the employer has "come across". But the employer will need to charge more for his wares and, to that extent, this tax is inflationary.
We propose an across the board tax of one cent per gallon. It ought to be paid by all, and would not impose a hardship, even on doctors who make emergency calls at night. I assure the minister that doctors are recompensed by OHIP in Ontario. When they receive a call in the middle of the night, they charge OHIP. They do not work for nothing.
It seems to me that the minister would collect just as much money if the tax were one cent a gallon across the board. The money could be raised by other means. Why not impose a tax on those who can afford to pay, on those who can afford to bet on the horses? All he need do is impose a tax on bets made at race tracks in this country, and he will raise a great deal of money. In the province of Ontario alone he could raise as much as $9 million a year from thoroughbred racing. If we extrapolate the figures to cover standard breeds and other forms of racing, I am sure the minister could raise $100 million by using this means. And by taxing people who could afford to play the horses, the minister would be acting fairly. He is not fair when he taxes those who must use their cars to go to work.
I submit that this tax will bear hardest on those workers who are not members of unions and who cannot afford to exert pressure on their employer to compensate them for the increase in cost of driving. Most workers are not represented by unions. Such workers are employed as waitresses, or in similar occupations; they are unorganized and, in most cases, do not earn very much. It may not be worth their while to go to work if they must pay this tax. As a result, they may give up their jobs. The unemployment insurance people will step in and the notation will appear on the appropriate documents "left for unjust cause." Tax those who can afford to go to the race track, not those who must drive to work.
But you have a large race track in your riding.

Yes, there is a race track in my riding. It seems to me that we should follow the precepts of our income tax system and charge those who can pay. The contribution of the taxpayer ought to reflect his ability to pay. I remind the hon. member for Peace River and others in his party of the slogan, "From each according to his ability to contribute." I put that in its proper capitalist context.
We therefore say, that the one cent per gallon tax across the board is more equitable, and is more in line with the provisions of our income tax system. The minister attempted to equate this regressive tax with our income tax structure. How can you equate this regressive tax with the income tax structure as, by and large, the income tax structure is more just and progressive? This particular excise tax is not a progressive tax. It is regressive, because it is to take from those who do not have and, invariably, will give to those who have.
I do not wish to delay hon. members as I know they are anxious to go on holiday; but so are the people in my

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Madam Chairman, we find ourselves in the official opposition facing a difficult choice. On the one hand, we think the amendment is a little ridiculous. On the other hand, the tax itself is a malignant one. So the choice is not an easy one. After some consideration we have decided to back the ridiculous amendment.

Madam Chairman, I appreciate the remarks of the hon. member for Peace River. We know perfectly well that the amendment will be defeated. Nevertheless, the amendment has a purpose which appears to me to be perfectly legitimate-it is to get the message through to the government and its advisers that this legislation is ridiculous in the first place.
It seems to me that hon. gentlemen opposite had better take another look at just what a sales tax is. The only element of fairness it contains is that those who can afford to buy most of the products, and who choose to do so, bear the heaviest burden of the tax. Those on low incomes who obviously purchase less of the commodity as a general rule, lose less of their disposable income in the form of sales tax. If a government applies a sales tax, it applies it across the board, or, at least, it provides for very limited exceptions-the handicapped might be excepted, for example, or those who have no choice but to buy the commodity concerned.
If the case in question involved the imposition of a tax of one cent a gallon on gasoline, everybody would pay it with, possibly, limited exceptions of those I mentioned. Those who bought the most would pay the most. It is rather like the sales tax on automobiles. The man who can only afford to buy a $4,000 car pays $200. But the person who wants to spend $20,000 on a car pays $1,000 in tax. To that extent, the tax provides for an element of ability to pay. But when the minister imposes a sales tax of ten cents a gallon and makes it possible for a certain group of people to write off some of it as an expense for income tax purposes, and, moreover, allows those in the higher income tax categories to apply for rebates, then he has destroyed whatever element of fairness there is in a sales tax. That is why we on this side have put forward an amendment to reduce the tax from ten cents a gallon to one cent a gallon.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Turner (Ottawa-Carleton) that Bill C-66, to amend the Excise Tax Act, be read the third time and do pass.

Madam Speaker, before moving a third reading amendment I should like to deal more or less precisely, depending on response from the other side, with the substance of this bill.
When the government announced that it was necessary to raise additional revenue in order to compensate for the loss of revenue from the export tax to meet the increasing cost of importing oil to the east coast, the members of our party hoped that this revenue would be raised in some equitable fashion. There is no argument at all that the government was in the position where it needed additional funds. The only issue was how it set about raising those funds. Of the options open to it, the government could not
29669-26Vi

July 29, 1975
Excise Tax Act
have chosen a more regressive means of raising the required money.
There are times when a user's tax is entirely appropriate and just. There are other times when a user's tax is just the opposite. In our view that is what we have at the present time. If it made any sense at all to argue that the vast majority of the people who drive automobiles have a genuine option in regard to driving them in terms of the necessity to get to and from work, then the argument put forward by the government might have made some sense. It would have made some sense to say that use of the automobile at this point in the twentieth century in Canada was a genuine option, and therefore if people chose to use that mode of transportation they should pay the additional tax that the government is imposing. However, just the opposite situation exists.
Most people in Canada go to and from work in an automobile because at this point in our history they have no alternative. Whether we are talking about tradesmen who have to go to construction sites many miles away from their place of work by an automobile because that is the only means, or whether we are talking about thousands of fishermen, longshoremen, loggers and miners who, by definition, have to travel to work by automobile, this whole range of workers are put in an unjust position by having to pay this tax.
I would also add to the list all people who live in suburban Halifax or suburban Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg, Edmonton, Calgary or Vancouver, people who are forced to live in the suburbs because housing prices in the centre of those cities are such that it is impossible for people of average or low income to maintain a residence there. The situation has been worsened by the lack of an urban policy, an urban transit policy which the government could have developed over the past two decades. This lack of policy has meant that people must travel by automobile. In order words, virtually every worker in Canada today is in the position of having to rely upon the automobile as the means of transportation for getting to and from work. Therefore we conclude, Madam Speaker, that this tax is a regressive form of raising revenue, one that places an unjust burden on people of average or low income, and we will have nothing to do with it.
As I said earlier this afternoon, the fair way, in fact the only way of raising the additional funds required is to impose a special income tax on Canadians of upper income, or to use money derived from general revenue which comes both from income tax sources, which are at least relatively progressive, and from taxes imposed upon the corporate sector. Either of these methods would have been just, compared with the method used by the government.
We in this party proposed a series of amendments at committee stage. They were amendments that would have provided exemptions for working Canadians who are required to go to and from work by automobile, as well as for handicapped Canadians, to name just two important categories. But the government has seen fit to reject both. Thus it is our intention at this stage to take the same course of action that we took at second reading stage, namely, to oppose the bill. If the government had shown some readiness to move at the committee stage and accept
some plausible and equitable amendments, then our position at this stage might have been something other than what is is. But as is characteristic of the Liberal party of Canada whenever it governs with a clear majority, the government has seen fit to go the way it determined upon originally, which is instead of distributing the economic burden in Canada in favour of the average or low income earner, to persits in aggravating the maldistribution of that economic burden.
This bill is something with which we will have nothing whatsoever to do. I therefore move, seconded by the non. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That Bill C-66 be not now read a third time but that it be read a third time this day six months hence.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I just want to say that we intend to support the amendment as my friends to my left supported us on the same amendment on second reading.
This bill has been some changes and some improvements. I must say that the improvements which I now see in the bill hardly justify the labour, energy, time and effort which have gone into this debate. Be that as it may, it is a little better bill than it was, but because it is not good enough we are going to vote for the proposed amendment.

Madam Speaker, in speaking in support of the motion for six months' hoist I must agree with the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) that a great deal of effort has been made by members of the opposition in an attempt to improve this bill and to rectify some of its obvious faults, yet little has been accomplished, considering the amount of effort put forward.
This situation is one that develops when we have a majority government. This may be something hon. members in the opposition will have to live with, but it is something that involves a much more important consideration. The suggestions and requests for improvement have been put forward by members of the opposition not for themselves but on behalf of a large segment of the Canadian public.
No tax bill is ever welcomed by the opposition, and it is not likely that a tax bill is welcomed by members of the government. There is a necessity to raise revenue through taxation. I am sure most members will agree that the government has a number of choices as to how it will raise that revenue required for the operations of the country. The government must find that money somewhere, and the choice of where is up to the cabinet.
We have been spoiled during the last eight or ten years in having had a number of minority governments. In such a situation a government is willing on occasion to listen to and consider propositions by the opposition, knowing full well that if it does not there will be an election. The government in the past few years has considered such propositions and, on occasion, accepted changes.
As far as the opposition is concerned, and also I suspect most backbenchers on the Liberal side, the main objection to this measure is in respect of the way the minister has

July 29, 1975

decided to raise $500 million in order to equalize prices in eastern and western Canada. He has chosen to do this through the imposition of a ten cents per gallon tax on gasoline. I think most members will agree with the principle enunciated by the minister.
I am always impressed by the minister's use of the English language and his facility for assuring us that he is concerned about the difficulties he faces in designing budgetary measures to solve the problems of inflation and unemployment. He has often said his primary concern is for the people of Canada, but that he has really not been able to do much about these problems of inflation and unemployment. I suggest the minister has been consistent in respect of Bill C-66. He has said that the measure is necessary to equalize the price of gasoline across Canada. By this bill I suggest he has not moved in any direction toward equalizing that price. I am sure that the price for grade two gasoline will be $1 a gallon in certain parts of Canada, and in the low 70-cents range in other parts. The minister has not in any way through this bill equalized the price.
What the minister is doing through this bill is raising money that will offset to some extent our loss in export revenues. He is accomplishing this not by a measure of equality but by the imposition of a ten cents tax which is unfair in that it will not apply to everyone.
A number of my colleagues have indicated several more equitable methods that could be used to distribute the burden of accomplishing what the minister wants to accomplish. One hon. member suggested a surcharge on income tax at the higher levels. The hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) was being unfair to the ponies in suggesting that perhaps the minister could collect the necessary revenue from betters at race tracks. A number of suggestions have been made, many of which are more equitable than the one proposed by the minister.
Because of its structure the income tax in this country is one of our most unfair taxes. Under this structure one never pays more than slightly less than 50 per cent. No matter how rich a person is, or how much money he receives per year, he only pays something less than 50 per cent under our income tax structure. This is unfair as well, because the level of income at which the tax reaches 46 per cent or 47 per cent is not very high. In many cases members of parliament with their salaries find themselves in that category. When you reach that relatively middle-class income you find the government has placed a limit on the amount it takes away, so our income tax structure is not fair.
To make the income tax system more equitable we should adopt a graduated scale which would continue beyond the present limit. It would then be possible in this country, as it is in others such as Sweden, to obtain our general revenues from corporate taxes, business taxes, and personal income taxes. Some countries have gone that far, adopting that honest and equitable type of tax, to look after almost all government expenditures, even those at the municipal level.
This country has not been that fair, and this minister certainly maintains the standard set by Liberal governments over the years in relation to our taxation structure. He has done so particularly in respect of this tax measure.
