The main part of the bill with which most of us are concerned is that portion relating to the ten cents per gallon tax on gasoline. The bill is not fair in respect of exemptions in that it is selective and applies only to certain individuals.
The minister should have given reasonable consideration to the suggestions put forward by the opposition, and I am sure he would have done so if we had a minority government.
A minority government is not good for the country.

Madam Speaker, my colleague on the other side of the House just made the profound statement that a minority government is not good for the country. That is a typical Liberal remark. In other words, if it is not good for the Liberals it is not good for the country.
Hear, hear!
I am happy to note that most Liberals agree. This means that if we had only one party in Canada and it were the Liberal party, then obviously we would have an ideal situation.
Right on.

This reminds me of Franco and a number of other such people. I have always been of the opinion that even when there has been a democratic socialist government in Canada it was not always right. In fact I found that the longer it stayed in power the less likely it was to be right.
In my opinion it has always been a good idea to have a strong opposition which brings forward alternatives. It is also a good idea to have an occasional change of government so that another party, which may feel the same as some of the Liberals that their ideas are the only right ideas, would be given an opportunity to put their ideas into effect for at least a short period.
Liberals in this case say that because the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) is a Liberal he cannot be wrong. We have watched the telegraphing between the floor and the gallery, a new method of operating the Department of Finance by what is called beaming information. I have news for some of the backbench Liberals. The Minister of Finance did not draft these proposals. He has been busy doing many other things, including running world financial organizations and representing his constituents. When they give this vote of confidence to the Minister of Finance they really are giving it to-
The birds in the roost up there.

-the gallery, the mandarins who wondered how they would raise this $500 million. They probably decided it would be a good idea to do it in the form of a gasoline tax. They probably also decided they should not affect big business and that they should place it in context. It really does not matter to a businessman whether or not the tax is imposed, just as it does not matter to people who are engaged in the professions. These people in any event will write off the tax. The people who will not have

an opportunity to write off this tax will be many members of parliament, the workers in this country, and the people in a few other categories, such as our senior citizens and others on fixed incomes.

And of course the dredging
companies.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to say a few words on the amendment which was proposed by the leader of my party which in effect calls for a six months postponement of this iniquitous bill which, as we have said time and time again in the House, is discriminatory with regard to a large group of working class Canadians. We have asked for a postponement of this bill for six months. I see the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) waving no. Well, he can wave no all he wants. I intend to take the full length of the time allotted to me on this amendment.
We have said in the debate that the bill which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) has proposed is in large part a method of collecting revenues so that the shortfall in the petroleum account can be met. We have said that

this measure is an iniquitous measure, that the method by which the government proposes to collect this $500 million is certainly not fair and not just to far too many Canadians. The exceptions which are made in the bill are such that it makes the bill inequitable. The exceptions do not change the lifestyle of the wealthy but they certainly place constrictions on the lifestyle of other Canadians.
It is all right for the Liberal members to mimick and to jeer, but in effect they must answer to their constituents as well. When they were parading before the Canadian public last July they were not so cocky about this whole matter of raising taxes. Now that they have a majority government they feel they can run roughshod over the opposition and over the Canadian people.
We have said that the bill is a piece of regressive legislation. For the Minister of Finance to rise in the House and put forward such a regressive bill and call it a progressive tax system is ludicrous. I find it difficult to understand how we can make such statements.
The Minister of Finance also said that he wants to change the lifestyle of Canadians and he wants people to conserve energy, he wants them to use less ostentatious cars and be more aware of the need to conserve energy. We have said, and I say it again, that if the government were to establish any credibility with the Canadian public it would have to conduct itself in such a manner that the Canadian public would say, "We will follow that example".
It was interesting to observe during the dinner recess tonight the great limousines lined up at the entrance to pick up the ministers-one minister sitting at the back of a big limousine to be driven to Confederation building, a distance of some 300 yards. If the government were itself aware of the need to conserve energy it would have the right to say to the Canadian people, "We will change your lifestyle". It is easy for them to say to the workers that they should organize car pools. I do not see the ministers organizing car pools. After all, it is not necessary to have 20 limousines to drive 20 ministers to the House every morning. Surely the minister could organize a car pool system. They all have telephones in their limousines.
Surely it is the responsibility of the government to practise what it preaches. It was interesting to hear the comments made by the Minister of Finance when he spoke yesterday evening in response to an amendment put forward by my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). The minister said:
But, to give a deduction of the expense of getting to work would be to give a tax subsidy to those who choose to drive rather than take public transport... to those who choose to live far from their place of work rather than close, and to those who choose to drive a large automobile rather than to those who drive a small one.
It is the height of hypocrisy and cynicism for any minister to say that people choose to live far from their place of work. In my constituency, as I have said many times in the House, people do not choose to live out in Alban, Noelvilie or Naughton. They live in those places because they can afford to buy a home there; they cannot buy a home in Sudbury where housing is too expensive.
A piece of land in Sudbury 55 feet wide and 125 feet deep costs $15,000. People cannot afford that kind of investment. They certainly do not choose to live in the

places I have named. They live there because of the price of houses, because instead of sewers there is a septic tank system, and because the taxes are not as high as in Sudbury. So it is not a matter of choosing; they are forced to live in such places as Killarney, Markstay Alban, St. Charles, Warren, and all these places with exotic names in my riding. People in my riding do not drink imported wines. We have said that this is an iniquitous bill because the government has imposed a restriction on people who live in certain parts of the country where a car is not a luxury but a necessity. On the other hand, the government has not provided those people with a public transit system to use. There is no public transit system in Nickel Belt. There is a public transit system of sorts in the city of Sudbury, but it does not extend beyond the borders of the city, so the people who live in the areas I have mentioned in my riding must use the automobile. There are also a large number of people in my riding, and in the ridings of other members of this House who are not within a union. When the union members' contracts come up, they can always negotiate to make up for the ten cent excise tax. It will be a tough fight, but that is another question. But there are a large number of people, mostly women, who work in my riding as waitresses or they sweep up hotel rooms, and they work for the minimum wage. They live in the outlying areas, and therefore a car is a necessity for them to maintain that employment. If it becomes unfeasible for them to continue that employment, they leave it, and they are then ineligible for unemployment insurance because they had no good reason for quitting.
My party has indicated that it will fight this iniquitous bill down to the wire, and we have done that right through this debate. As a matter of fact, as part of our responsibility as members of parliament and as a party, we made proposals to the government. We have proposed alternatives. For example, we proposed that the rebates be applied to those who must use their cars to and from work. We have also suggested that the handicapped be eligible for the rebate when such disabled persons use cars or are driven to their place of employment, for enjoyment or whatever. We also proposed, since we lost those amendments, that the excise tax be reduced from ten cents to one cent per gallon and be applied universally. What does the minister say about allowing workers to claim the rebate, those workers who have to use their cars to go back and forth to work? The minister said, and I quote:
I do not deny for a minute that there will be cases of hardship. Unfortunately, there is no equitable way to cope with these situations which is administratively feasible.
Are we to believe that this government, which has been in power for a long, long time, is incapable of devising a system whereby it can discriminate and select those of the taxpayers who are using their cars to go to and from work? Are we to say that this country, which was capable of building the tallest freestanding building in Toronto in the guise of the CN tower and which is planning some fantastic buildings for the Olympics in 1976 is incapable of coming up with a bureaucratic system which can separate those who use their cars to go to and from work from those who use their cars for enjoyment? Statistics show that the percentage of those who own cars which are used for frivolous reasons, for enjoyment or for holidays, is very small compared to those who use their cars to travel to work. In this society we have built our community around the automobile.

The minister talks about conservation. Just the other day I was watching television, and a commercial came on for, I think, Texaco. Texaco is encouraging consumers to purchase its gasoline, and if customers accumulate so many coupons from a particular dealer, they receive glassware, cutlery and tea sets. Does that fit in with some kind of conservation policy? I dare say that 99 per cent of the drivers in this country already have decided on a particular brand of gasoline, so it is not to attract those who use Gulf gasoline to start using Texaco gasoline. It is obviously geared to increasing the usage of that particular brand of gasoline. That is what the advertisements are directed toward. It seems to me that that kind of gimmickery is the gimmickery which ought to be taxed, and not consumers who must use fuel to get to work.
It seems to me that if the government has a conservation policy, it should be reflected in the total spectrum of what is going on in this country. How can we have oil companies pushing consumption and, on the other hand, the government talking about conservation of energy? The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand)-and this is another case of trying to change the lifestyle of the Canadian people-said that transportation is in a mess. He certainly was not kidding. What is the government trying to do? I have said before-and it seems to me that hon. members have not taken it seriously-that we do not have a nationally-owned railway company. The CN does not have one passenger car on order. Are we trying to develop interurban transportation? Are we trying to get people off airplaines and on to railway cars? Not on your life, Mr. Speaker. What does this government do? It is prepared to spend $100 million at Terminal 2, at Toronto airport, building more parking lots. How does one reconcile what the government says about conservation of energy and changing the lifestyle of the people? Are we trying to improve the railway service in this country? No, we are not.
The government built the STOL airport here for people flying from Ottawa to Montreal. People can be moved by rail just as economically or more so. The railway is a far more economical method of transporting people than flying. As a matter of fact, statistics show that moving people by airplane over a distance of 500 miles is not at all economical. Air Canada reported a loss of $19 million last year on the Toronto-Ottawa-Montreal route, yet we see big ads by Air Canada today which is selling two seats out of three, leaving the one in the middle empty. How can the government talk about changing lifestyles, economy and conservation of energy when it turns around and does such stupid things? How can the government be credible to the Canadian people?
It has been said that television ought to be brought into the House of Commons. I look forward to the day when the Minister of Finance can make hypocritical statements as he did last night when he said that we could not have a bureaucratic structure which could separate those who are using cars to travel to and from work from those who do not. How does the minister propose to do this with regard to doctors who are called out in the middle of the night when he says he cannot do it for carpenters and plumbers because they are on contracts? So are doctors. They are on contract with OHIP. If they go out in the middle of the night, they can put in a bill to OHIP for their services. No

one is quarrelling about that, but we want the same privilege to be extended to people in the working class.
We have proposed a reasonable amendment. Every member in this corner of the House agrees that it is. There is not one here who disagrees.
I do.

That hon. member is a Liberal transplanted to these benches.
We have suggested that this bill be hoisted for six months-and I think that is a wise suggestion-so that the government can rethink its position and reconsider the inequities in this particular tax bill. I recall that in the last election the Liberal candidate in Sudbury was promising "We want the railway tracks out of the city. We are going to push hard for it." The Liberal candidate in Nickel Belt was saying, "We want them in Nickel Belt." That says something about the transportation policy of the government. The government has shown how phony the arguments have been. We have made some excellent suggestions about how it could collect taxes. We suggested it would be more fair to take the money out of general revenues, and those who do not own cars could be compensated by an allowance on their income tax. It is supposed to be a great system. Those who have money should pay, and those with the least income should pay less. It seems to me that that kind of progressive income tax structure is better than this excise tax.
The minister has been given some other very good suggestions by this party. I have suggested that people who go to the race track should pay another three cents on every dollar they bet. At the moment the tax is 15 cents on the dollar. We could pull in another $9 million from the Ontario Jockey Club through the thoroughbred flat racing and I have not even included standard breds. There are many tracks in this country and on any given night the amount wagered is from $215,000 to $400,000.
We have suggested that corporations that have deferred their taxes to the tune of $7 billion should pay an interest rate of 10 per cent. That seems fair in view of the fact that they have enjoyed the benefits of deferring payment of their taxes. I cannot defer my tax nor can you, Mr. Speaker, so it seems fair that they should pay interest on that loan.
We have made constructive suggestions to the government but they have fallen on deaf ears. We have repeated them many times hoping to puncture the wax that has accumulated in those ears, but to no avail.
When we were campaigning last summer the Liberals promised an urban transit system. They have forgotten it now that they have a majority. They have derailed the Canadian people and pushed them all on to airplanes. Not too many people in Nickel Belt can afford to fly; they are not on a travel expense account. They have not got government planes to fly them around, like the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has his

I know other members of my party will have strong words to say in support of the amendment. I urge hon. members on all sides to support our amendment. wrong. Well, Mr. Speaker, the population is not as stupid as that.
What I fail to comprehend is the unanimous attitude of government members. Unanimity! Not one dares speak against the government. Or rather I can explain it by the party's dictature in caucus, a fact that I have always denounced in this House. Such are the results of a majority government. Today, the Liberal government is imposing this unpopular tax because it knows that the next elections are far away. And I am willing to bet that on the eve of the next elections, this same government will remove this tax to please the voters of this country. All Liberal partisans will forget the date of June 24, 1975, not because it is the French Canadians' day, but because it was the day a ten-cent tax on a gallon of gas was forced on those unable to pay it.
Mr. Speaker, I hope this marathon of debates will end and I urge all opposition parties to vote. That is the game of democracy and I hope that tonight we shall keep that democracy alive in giving members of Parliament this freedom. Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on the amendment on third reading to explain why we feel this bill should sit for another six months to give the government time to bring in another piece of legislation which would raise the amount of money we agree is required, and do so in a much better way.
I am not one of those who think the continuance of this debate is an exercise in game playing or anything else. If I did not feel strongly that this is the wrong way to raise the amount of money the government requires I would not be on my feet tonight. This would be the case whatever party happened to be in power.
That is hard to believe.

We have suggested ever since the bill came in that when a given amount of money is required to accomplish a national goal the government has a duty to put forward legislation which is fair to the greatest possible number of people from the Atlantic to the Pacific. We contend that the legislation before us not only fails to do this but actually moves in the opposite direction. I shall not go into all the details, no doubt to the relief of hon. members across the way. They know those arguments. I will simply ask them this: if they were sitting as members of a municipal council, or of a school board, or of a provincial legislature, would they countenance the imposition of a tax for a specific purpose which bore most heavily on those least able to pay it?
I listened with a good deal of incredulity this afternoon to the discussion on who might be excused from the payment of this ten cents per gallon tax. In itself, ten cents on a gallon of gasoline or on whatever amount of gas a person may use in a year is not an extraordinarily large sum. But in terms of the kind of parliament this parliament is likely to be, it is important. We have only been here one year and there are three more to go. So the issue is important in terms of whether or not parliament is in fact the body governing our country.
I am shocked to think that members of parliament sitting in this chamber would turn their backs on a proposal to relieve handicapped people from the obligation of paying this tax. It was bad enough that the Liberals should have stood up against that proposal. The worst tragedy was when the Official Opposition not only withdrew their amendment, which was a darned good one, but abstained from voting on a subsequent amendment to exempt handicapped people totally from paying tax on any gas they might use whether for pleasure, attending clinics, or going to and from work. These great friends of the workers and the common people in the Official Opposition failed to vote. I wish the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) had been here; I do not think he would have liked it.
There are errors of omission on the part of all members of opposition parties. There is only the odd occasion in the course of the life of a majority government when an issue arises on a matter of principle on which we can all fight to the line. I want to say there are even some people here in my own caucus who are not here and who should be here. While I admit to, and confess, the failings in my own ranks, I want to say to the members supporting the government who have this traditional Liberal state of mind and attitude, that they are the only ones selected to govern, they are the only ones who know, they are the only ones "who have all the answers"-if once in a while they sit in opposition it is only a temporary aberration and loss of sense on the part of the voters!
But in a traditional British parliamentary system I would expect that even members on the government side in the British House of Commons would have risen and voted against some of the measures in this bill. But not a sound out of one of them, unless they are nattering while signing letters or standing behind the curtains or sneaking in from behind the curtains like sheep to vote.

We have presented at least 12 other ways to raise $350 million in 1975 and to raise the $500 million to $525 million required in the 12 months of 1976. All of these ways would have ensured a great deal more equity, fairness and justice than the provisions of this bill. Some of them would have been proposed at Liberal party conventions or even by a minority Liberal government. But when in the majority, they know everything. There is not a thing they can do wrong. They are the only ones fit to govern. I hear the hon. lady across the way lightly pounding her desk. I am glad she only pounded her desk lightly; I know her heart was not in it. If she will pound it harder, I will have some other words to say.
To collect the $525 million for the oil consumption fund in a manner which would bring about a genuine equalized price from coast to coast, and to collect it in a way that would be fair and just, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) could have done any one of the following. I have not seen any editorials or news stories carrying these proposals, but personally I do not worry about that. That is a reflection on the members of the press gallery who are not much different from members of the House of Commons. They, too, are worried about getting off to the lake, or going fishing, or getting together with the wife and kids this summer. It would be very nice, however, if the media were not captives of the kind of system under which we operate. It would be very nice if on their own hook, without waiting for or relying upon members of parliament, they had suggested to the government in their editorials, columns or news stories more equitable and just ways in which this money could have been raised.
What I say does not apply just to this bill. Budget bills are nothing more than the result of a budget, and this budget was one with which the minister should not have bothered. Let me illustrate. We could raise the $525 million which is required in the calendar year 1976 and the $350 million that is required in part of 1975 in a manner that is just, one based on ability to pay, if we had said to individual taxpayers that each of them with a taxable income in excess of a certain amount would pay a 3 per cent higher rate of effective tax, or that the corporations would pay a 10 per cent higher effective tax rate. Or we could have had a combination of both and levied an additional 5 per cent corporate tax rate and a l'/2 or 2 per cent higher individual tax rate. Then, the burden of raising this money would have been spread among those with the ability to pay.
Instead of that, the government chose to levy a ten cents a gallon excise tax. In levying this tax, the minister provides in the bill that if those in the higher income brackets are in business or in the professions, they must keep records as a basis for claiming this expenditure as an expense item to be deducted from their income tax. If they are in a 25 per cent or 30 per cent tax bracket, then they will have the benefit of paying less taxes as the result of having deducted their total purchases of gasoline or any other legitimate business expense.
In addition to that, a professional person engaged in commercial enterprise, as the legislation so describes, may apply for a rebate. The minister has told the House that a doctor, lawyer, architect, chartered accountant and so

Let me deal now with those I referred to earlier, the people who can least afford to pay the tax. I realize that not very much money is involved during the course of a year-the sort of amount that one would spend, say, in the parliamentary restaurant or in some fancy restaurant in downtown Ottawa on a given evening. But it is the people on fixed incomes and the pensioners who, as usual under free enterprise government tax systems, will pay a disproportionate share of the tax burden. An old age pensioner who might use his car three times a week will contribute anywhere from $1 to $3 a month by way of excise tax. This will amount to as much as, or a little more than, the last cost of living escalation of the old age pension, which I think was $2.33 a month.
Every member of the House has in his constituency old age pensioners who drive automobile for what the Minister of Finance and hon. members opposite call pleasure. Let me examine this so-called pleasure. These old age pensioners make one trip a week to buy groceries. They have no other way of transporting themselves than by the automobile, but the Minister of Finance calls that pleasure. They make two or three trips a month to the doctor's office, and according to the Minister of Finance that, too, is pleasure driving. They make two or three trips a year to visit their children or grandchildren; again according to the Minister of Finance that is pleasure. There are no rebates for such expenditure. We pleaded with the government to exempt those people who are drawing old age pensions and the guaranteed income supplement. More particularly, we asked the government to exempt those who are drawing old age pensions and are liable for some income tax on income they receive over and above the old age pensions.
Can it be classed as driving for pleasure when these people drive their automobiles 8,000 or 10,000 miles a year to pick up their groceries, go to the doctor's office, or to visit their children and grandchildren? This does not involve a large amount of money in each of these individual cases and it is not a large amount in the total financial picture of this country. Surely this legislation is an indication that we are travelling down the same road we have been travelling all along.
There is another way the government could have raised this revenue. The hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes), and the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) have mentioned this method. I will not refer again to the race tracks and horses, but will refer only to deferred taxes. There are deferred taxes lying on the books of this country amounting to $7 billion. Would it not be reasonable to charge a small interest rate on these deferred taxes, perhaps 7.5 per cent? This would be a much lower rate than the rest of us are paying on money that we owe. This would raise the $525 million the Minister of Finance must have next year.

If we were to put out $7 billion in mortgages for people who want to buy homes there would be a cry of protest and outrage from the financial institutions, the realtors, and the developers. If we were to put out $7 billion in interest free loans for the construction of homes there would be a great cry of outrage, yet we carry on the books of this nation $7 billion in deferred taxes.
This party has moved that this bill not be read now a third time but that it be read six months hence for a very good reason, and we will move the same motion in respect of any other budget bills the government might want to bring in this fall. If hon. members are worrying now about a summer recess they should start worrying as well about a Christmas and New Year's recess.
This bill imposes a penalty on those people who earn wages and salaries whether or not they belong to unions. If they live five miles or more from their places of work and drive that distance, in the course of 12 months they will have paid back every dollar of tax credit they may have gained from the $150 allowed for the cost of tools and other expenses. If those people saved $30 in income tax, this measure will take more than that amount back.
In addition, this ten cents a gallon tax will take back from the working people who drive several miles to and from their places of employment all the benefit of the tax credit each taxpayer is receiving as a result of the first $50 credit, then the $100 credit, and then the $150 credit. Incidentally, this is now back to $100. This measure will take back from those workers every dollar gained from that tax credit.
One of my friends opposite sent me a chart which is being circulated among the Liberal caucus. The way it reads, if you drive 7,000 miles a year averaging 15 miles per gallon, this amounts to only 469 gallons which, at 10 cents a gallon, amounts to $46.90. This is the chart those Liberal members are passing around, I presume to salve their own consciences. This is a nice little chart and very convenient, but they have forgotten a few things in this chart they are passing around while patting each other on the back.
If you drive 7,000 miles a year to and from work, the ten cents a gallon tax on the gasoline amounts to $46.90. This proves one of the points I have just made. It takes away every nickel these people gain on their income tax as a result of the $150 deduction for expenses. In fact it takes away more than they gain.
The Liberal members have forgotten a couple of other things when circulating these cooked-up figures. They have forgotten also that on August 15, or very shortly thereafter, there will be another five cents a gallon increase in the cost of gasoline because of the increase in oil prices. Those members have also forgotten that when the companies pass on the ten cents and five cents increases, the distributors, bulk dealers, and retailers will all take their percentage of mark-up so that the total final increase in gasoline prices will be somewhere between 18 cents and 22 cents a gallon. This will mean in turn that people will lose everything they gained as a result of the $100 tax credit. It will have been taken away from them by this one silly and dumb bill.

The Minister of Finance could have raised this revenue, which we all agree the government must have in order to treat people relatively equal across the country, in a manner which would have been more equitable and just. The minister has failed to do so.
The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) paid a mild compliment to the government today for accepting a couple of minor changes to the bill. The government has failed to accept the suggestion that it withdraw the bill entirely. It has failed to agree to some of our suggestions on a better way to raise this required revenue. It was my hope that some of these suggestions would have come from the hon. member for Skeena (Mrs. Campagnolo), the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt), the hon. member for York South (Mrs. Appolloni), or from Liberal members of parliament who represent ridings in highly industrialized areas with a large working force, which is that segment of the population that will pay the largest proportion of this tax. These suggestions did not come from those hon. members. In any event, the government refused to accept the proposed amendments.
Let me say to hon. members opposite that they are not always 100 per cent right. Their party is not the only party fit to govern, and those hon. members are not always infallible in the legislation they bring forward. The government weakens the democratic process of our parliamentary system when it flies in the face of the general public with something like this that is so obviously unfair and unjust.
I suggest the motion before us is one that warrants a vote. It puts forward what we have been trying to say about this particular bill, and what I suspect we will be saying about subsequent bills arising from the last budget in the months ahead. If this debate has done nothing else I hope it has taught hon. members opposite a lesson. I hope they will remember the lesson when they are in caucus and in committee, and when they are giggling together in the backbenches and behind the curtains. I hope they have learned something from this exercise. I hope this lesson will be reflected in the next piece of legislation that comes before this House arising from the latest budget. More important, I hope the minister has received the message.
The message we have tried to put forward is that you do not place the largest part of the tax burden on those who are least able to pay, while at the same time letting those who can pay off the hook. How any self-respecting member of parliament can hold still for that kind of nonsense is just beyond me.
This is a bad bill and this is the wrong way of raising this revenue. I only wish this bill had come before us some 18 months ago. We would then have gone through the usual process of having Liberals come over here behind the curtains clutching Conservatives, New Democrats, and Creditistes by the elbow and asking them what they would like to have in this bill or what it would take to get it through quickly. On such occasions butter would not melt in their mouths. Then they are the greatest democrats one could find.
Now the arrogance rises to the surface again. It would
seem that they are the only ones fit to govern. The arro-

gance is apparent in their expressions, in their smiles, and in their jeers. They meet us in the elevator at the fifth floor by the cafeteria and ask us to shut off the debate because they have an engagement or want to go to the lake. Their arrogance shows up in the way they talk, smile, and jeer. They do not move amendments or speak the way they want to speak. They are the government. If they really want to do something about parliamentary practice, here is the opportunity. They might not have another opportunity for a year or two. This is an opportunity for ordinary members of parliament-they are all nice, bright fellows-to say that the method being followed through this bill is the wrong method. No one is perfect. That might be news to my hon. friends opposite.
Members opposite should say that this bill is wrong, and give it a six months' hoist. If the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the government House leader, and the Minister of Finance would hoist this bill and then come back in two or three weeks with a new piece of legislation to raise the revenue required in a fair and equitable manner, they would be surprised at how fast that legislation would go through. They would realize there is more involved in parliament than just having a majority. They should think more about the people who sent them here. They should think about the people who must drive to the hospitals and to physiotherapy treatment centres. These are the people who must drive cars and yet they are being excluded from the rebate. Do any of you have the courage to speak for the people who elected you? That applies to all of us in every part of this House.

Madam Speaker, I was speaking of everyone in this House, and when I was asking the members of this House to speak up for those who sent them here, I was including you, Madam Speaker, in those remarks. I want to conclude by saying to my hon. friends-and I mean friends-
Oh, oh!
You should use another term.

My hon. friends might feel I have overstated the case or have become carried away. If they do, I apologize, but I do not apologize for the sincerity of my argument. In fact I am proud of the fact that we are still sitting here tonight in a whatever one might call it-a futile or last ditch effort. I meant every single word I said. Hon. members on all sides of the House have an opportunity to ask the government to take back this bill and present another one designed to raise the same amount of money in a more equitable and just manner, and not to fly in the face of principles which I know my hon. friends across the way hold dear.

Madam Speaker, I wish to take only a few minutes of the House's time this evening to refer again to the amendment I presented this afternoon in an opportunity to obtain a rebate for the handicapped people. The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) expressed puzzlement that we did

July 29, 1975
Excise Tax Act
not vote for his belated amendment. On behalf of my party I chose instead to trade off an amendment that the government could easily have defeated for a commitment from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) to achieve the same aim by regulation. It would seem to me that this was much better than an effort to score debating points.
It seemed to me I should accept the firm commitment of one of the most honourable of the Queen's Privy Councillors, the Minister of Finance, to bring forth similar regulations. Our party could have won the debate, but the handicapped would not have been given the right to a rebate from this inequitable tax. An elderly constituent once told me that a member of parliament could accomplish a lot if he did not worry too much about who received the credit. I recommend my constituent's advice to the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre.
Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, it seems to me that Bill C-66 has been like a bingo game with the famous No. 66. There has been a great deal of discussion and debate in an attempt to have the government realize the wisdom of withdrawing the bill, to have the government approve amendments, or even to have the government itself bring in amendments. It is regretted that the government has adopted such an arbitrary and harsh method to extract funds from the people of our country.
I must agree with most of the remarks made by members of the opposition parties in the House. However, they have fallen on deaf ears. It would be appropriate now to direct pressure to another part of the anatomy. There are other alternative methods to raise revenue, but the Liberal government evidently is not prepared to show leadership in relieving the country of the burden caused by the crisis which faces us. The day Bill C-66 is proclaimed will be a sad day for this country and for many of its citizens. Nevertheless the bill and the amendments have been debated relentlessly.
The bill should never have been presented. It should have been withdrawn. It is imperfect. I am not too sure that it is not contrary to the provisions of Magna Carta in that it gives authority to the governor in council to tax without representation. That is what taxation by decree or order in council is. At this time, however, it appears to me that it is time to give everyone in the House an opportunity see where they stand on the amendment, on the bill and on the motions before the House. I have the impression that this session has lasted about ten months and most members of parliament in the House are on edge. Therefore, I propose the following motion, seconded by the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard):
That the House sit beyond the ordinary hour of adjournment this evening for the following purpose: To complete the debate and to complete all action on amendments and all proceedings and stages of Bill C-66, and act to amend the Excise Tax Act.

It is normal that after ten months of session, each of us would like to return in his constituency to spend a few days with the family, which is good for every Canadian. Parliamentarians are also Canadian citizens, and of course, they want to be able to live for a few days, a few weeks.
Madam Speaker, I hear members on the government side say that I am saying nice things. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) is giving me the signal to cut it short. There is good sense in that. But the fact remains that we are not here to have fun. We are here to govern.
If we recognize that the Liberal party is responsible for introducing laws to Parliament, I recognize that Parliament is responsible for passing the bills that are put to it. We are not here to oppose the government systematically. Come on! We are here to represent part of the population, and it has been proved that the opposition represents 57 per cent of the population; that part of the population feels saturated with taxes; the time has come to find new formulas, and I believe hon. members, as a group, feel somewhat responsible for finding them.
I see the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Tessier) go through the same motion as our grandmothers when they unwinded a skein of wool. I do not understand what he means by that, but it does not matter: I am not here for that. Over the past few days, I have had the opportunity to meet and talk with my constituents, school boards and other organizations. I have conducted this study in a serious and responsible manner and I have come to the conclusion that most people are against Bill C-66, especially in connection with the famous 10-cent tax on gas.

I want to fulfil my duties as the elected representative of a group of people who are willing to assume their responsibilities, accept their tax burden for the administration of our country, but not blindfolded. They want explanations. Why does the government insist on imposing a 10-cent tax on every gallon of gas which will be used in Canada? They want to know from the government what regulations will be edicted following the adoption of this bill? They want to know whether it is the members of Parliament or bureaucrats and technocrats who are in charge of this country and who will later on edict regulations and determine what classes of people will be considered as businessmen, and if such and such person will be deemed to be in business.
And I think it is important for the population to know that the members of parliament, their representatives, knew what they were doing when they voted that bill, and that is why I insist again tonight, Madam Speaker that the procedure be modified, that we get out of that system whereby members of Parliament adopt a legislation and bureaucrats and technocrats decide to interpret members' will.
I am tired of that, I am disgusted of that, and I want to say it tonight, at the third reading stage of that important Bill C-66, so that it will be known once and for all. I must commend the President of the Privy Council (M. Sharp), whom I see at his seat tonight, despite the length of the session, for still being here tonight to listen to members' representations. Let's adopt once and for all in the committee on procedure and organization a different method so that regulations that will be voted be enacted after that bill has been adopted. Because the government has a majority, they are sure the bill will be adopted. Come on! But we will not be mistaken for a bunch of dummies. We know that government members are a majority. Maybe several of them will tell their constituents tomorrow: "We did not agree with the tax on gasoline, but as things stood, there was a case of absolute necessity and we had to say yes. We were asked to stick together". Well, we already know that this legislation will be passed by the government majority, but I strongly doubt that the people in my constituency will congratulate the Liberal party. I guess on the contrary they will ask the Liberals to help them, to give them directions as to how they can get a refund on the tax.
It is extraordinary to hear the remarks of ordinary people. They wonder: Will I manage to get a refund? If they accept to pay that tax, they keep hoping they will get a refund, but what about the small taxpayer, the factory worker, the one who drives from Berthier or Montmagny to the shipyard in Lauzon, who has to drive some 35 or 40 miles, what about the worker from Montmagny who goes to work on American sites, in the state of Maine, as a hewer of wood, who has to pay for the gasoline he needs to get there? Will he be glad that this legislation was passed, whereas in fact the government could find different means if they sincerely wanted to alleviate the burden of taxes on the shoulders of Canadians taxpayers? Let us concentrate on large corporations and let us investigate all their fraudulent schemes to cheat our income tax legisla-

Madam Speaker, I hear colleagues in this House who seem to disagree but who deep inside know that I am telling the truth. They know I have the courage to say in this House what is actually happening and there is an injustice done to individuals, small businesses, workers, all those who labour day after day to earn a living and serve the people. Madam Speaker, that has lasted long enough. We should demand from large corporations the same discipline, the same claims, the same procedures so they will file honest reports with the Department of Revenue and if they owe $1 million they will pay $1 million, if they owe $2 million they will pay $2 million, just like we demand of the taxpayer who owes $600 that he pay $600.
Well, Madam Speaker, I see my colleagues opposite find that funny. We are not here to administer like a gang of jokers, you know that. Mr. Speaker, I am happy to speak at the third reading stage to express the opinion of my party as concerns this bill. I want to say that we are not more in favour of the bill at this time than we were at the second reading stage. In spite of the efforts made by the opposition to change the opinion of the government or the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) and in spite of some amendments, I wonder how this bill can be applied.
We can read the following on page 2 of the bill:
Where gasoline has been purchased by
(b)	a person for commercial or business purposes,
Who will determine if the gasoline was purchased for commercial or business purposes?
Paragraph (c) says:
(c)	a farmer for farming purposes,
Who will determine if the gasoline was purchased by a farmer or by someone who works in a city and farms part-time? Once again, as I said this afternoon, a public servant will determine what will happen. What will be the percentage of gasoline purchased by a farmer, by a labourer, by a manual worker or by another type of worker?
Paragraph (d) on the same page reads as follows:
(d)	a fisherman, hunter or trapper for commercial fishing, hunting
or trapping,
Once again, Madam Speaker, it is impossible to determine how much gasoline such a person will have purchased during a fiscal year in his capacity as fisherman, trapper and so on.
I would like to say that our party, the Social Credit Party of Canada, is still against this bill because it is the gift of the Liberal party to the poor workers who do not have one cent left to travel and to go to work. They do not have these 10 cents a gallon that they will have to pay on gasoline to travel every morning and every night. Therefore, the bill penalizes heavily the heads of families who cannot afford to pay for rent increases, increases of this and increases of that. Cost of living increases have emptied their pockets. They must leave home in the morning to go to work. The gift of the Liberal party to the Canadian voters is a great deception, Madam Speaker, and I believe that it is an indictment against the Liberal party.
Madam Speaker, in constituencies like mine, people earn their living underground, working in mines, breathing dust 24 hours a day and on any of the three 8-hour shifts, and they never go to bed at the same hour from one week to the next. It is thus appalling to see the government charging 10 cents a gallon of gasoline to miners who drive to work and who have the guts to work in these circumstances.
I think this is a nonsense, an impropriety, and I believe this legislation is not even workable from a legal standpoint or even from an honest standpoint, because it allows too much latitude to the official who has to determine how
Excise Tax Act
much gas goes for pleasure driving and how much for driving to work.
The foreman, for instance, who might be my boss tomorrow on the site where I would have to work since I might become a worker-and I speak for the workers in my constituency-will be entitled to a 10 cents a gallon tax rebate because he is a foreman and is thus driving for business purposes.
Me, the poor guy who earns $6,000, $7,000 a year, I shall pay, like him who makes around $25,000 or $30,000, 10 cents a gallon for gasoline. I think it is dishonest and unfair. This is all I wish to say. I do not wish to extend the debate, but I wish to say this: We do not agree anymore today than we did yesterday. What the minister did shyly under the pressure of the opposition does not satisfy us at all and I think that this bill on which we are going to vote on third reading is disastrous for the financial situation of the poor worker, the wallet of the small earner, of the head of a family, the man who does not have one more penny to spend to drive to work but who has the guts to do it.
The day will come, Madam Speaker, when those people who are too big-hearted will stop thinking as they do now and say: "Rather than working for nothing we are going to live on welfare". I hope that this day is still far away but the more bills of this kind we pass the sooner this day will come. Madam Speaker, in all fairness, I must say that this bill is impossible to apply and will be very unfair to some people. We shall have to establish the quantity of gas they bought to travel to work or for commercial purposes.
I said this afternoon that an hon. member or senator who is the owner or president of a business owning four vehicles or who bought one vehicle from his company with credit cards registered with that same vehicle will come to Ottawa and will buy gas with his company's credit cards and he will get 19 cents a mile to travel and this measure will give him a rebate on the 10 cents a gallon tax on gasoline. Who will establish what we should take off and what percentage of that gasoline he bought for his business or to travel to Parliament? It will not be easy! Can you imagine a senior civil servant having to decide what to do? I say that there is a very important thing.
In my opinion, a bill should at least be applicable. In all fairness, this bill cannot be applicable, because, as I said a moment ago, it gives too much latitude to the officials who will decide who is to pay the tax and who is not.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-LEVY CHARGED ON MANUFACTURING MILK-GOVERNMENT POSITION

speakeroldname: Mr. A. D. Alkenbrack (Frontenac-Lennox and Addington):
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-LEVY CHARGED ON MANUFACTURING MILK-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise again tonight in the adjournment debate to speak on behalf of the dairy farmers of Canada, some of whom are my constituents trying to earn a living in the dairy industry. I join a long line of colleagues in this House-the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday), the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle), the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise), the hon. member for Hastings (Mr. Ellis), and the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Beaudoin)-in protest against the increasing levies being imposed on dairy farmers to pay for the inefficiency and uneconomic powdered milk export programs of the government.
Many of the statistics have been read into the record concerning this problem. I will not go into the statistics tonight because I wish to make my point regarding export markets, as I believe our efforts should be aimed in that direction if we are to avoid further cost to the Canadian consumer for dairy products.
Correspondence we have received from the Ontario Milk Marketing Board, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the dairy farmers of Canada and from all the county milk committees of Ontario has expressed great concern. Their sound arguments are generally that our dairy producers do not think it fair that they should be called upon to bear all the burden of the deficits on powdered milk exports. Of course this situation is caused by the fact that the milk producing member nations of the European Economic Community each subsidize their dairy farmers to a degree which protects them from all costs and deficits connected with the export sale of powdered milk, it being the least and last residue of the industry.
Then the EEC headquarters in turn, I believe, protects and reimburses the governments of each one of those nations. Unfortunately that is not the case here, and the Canadian dairy farmer now faces the full onslaught of the competition of the European Economic Community and is now actually subsidizing it to the tune of another 45 cents as of July 1, and I am informed that will amount to another $250 million per year when the 45 cents per hundred is applied to our total national production.
It was only last spring when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), amid much publicity, conferred with the mem-
July 29, 1975	COMMONS DEBATES	__________________8059
bers of the EEC and was reported to have made overtures for contractual agreements with the big nine, but he did not put one word in on behalf of the Canadian dairy farmer. No, we get the back of the hand of the EEC.
Continuing the point I wish to make, what about these loudly touted contractual agreements by the Prime Minister on his visit to the EEC? Was there any economic strategy whatsoever to the representations of the Prime Minister? Apparently not. Can the government not direct its marketing efforts on powdered milk to other markets in countries now receiving bounteous and almost free Canadian aid, for example, the $10 million soft loan to Cuba which I opposed in February and May when the government was giving Cuba $10 million cash at 3 per cent interest for 30 years, with no repayment for the first seven years? Why does the government not make that contribution in powdered milk instead of cash wrested from the taxpayers of this country, some of whom are the dairy farmers of Canada?
What is happening at the present time? I know there is a large surplus of powdered milk accumulating in the world. The European Common Market has 700,000 tons of it. Today's Montreal Star carries an article which demonstrates that the European Economic Community is in command of this situation and that the Trudeau government is not even trying to compete with it in getting rid of skim milk surpluses. The article is headlined "Market may sell Egypt $385 million food surplus", and I quote from it:
Brussels-The Common Market commission is negotiating a controversial deal with Egypt involving the sale of about $385 million worth of EEC food surpluses.
According to Abdel Rohman El Chazli, the Egyptian supply minister, the package would include 1 million tons of wheat, 75,000 tons of sugar and 23,000 tons of dairy products.
In addition, 20,000 tons of the EEC's mountain of skimmed milk powder-now standing at 700,000 tons-will be given to Egypt as food aid.
Egypt is desperately short of both food and cash and it is likely that the deal will be financed by credits recently granted to Cairo by Kuwait and Saudi Arabia. However, if it goes through, EEC farmers also will reap considerable benefits.
The EEC sees to it that its dairy farmers receive the benefits of its world trade strategy. Hon. members will note the article mentions EEC finances by credits extended to needy countries.
To finish making my point there is another item in today's Montreal Gazette headlined "Half million Angolans face starvation." Why could Angola not use some of our powdered milk to feed its half million refugees?
Let us survey the problems of CIDA. Wherever this agency extends large amounts of cash in aid to needy countries, wherever possible let skim milk powder be part of that cash. That would reduce the current load on the dairy farmer who now takes the penalty of 90 cents per hundred. In my county there are many producers who say that the latest 45 cent levy will cost them at least $5 per day. One industrial milk producer near Napanee told me it currently costs him $160 per month.
There is one more point to be made on behalf of the dairy producers. They abide by the first 45 cents levy, which went on the first of the year, but they strongly protest the application of the second 45 cents levy in the middle of the year. With dairy farms the calendar year is
Adjournment Debate
their fiscal year, generally speaking. They have commitments made on that basis that they must keep, commitments to many accounts, mainly financial, and to make another unexpected levy on them out of thin air the first of July in mid-year is very unfair to the industry. In many, many cases it is going to be a matter of the knife edge of profit or loss, but mostly loss on the year's operations.
I respectfully ask the minister to examine that 20 per cent portion of the formula laid down. As reported at page 7960 in Hansard of July 25, his parliamentary secretary said in reference to the 20 per cent margin:
This is an advantage that allows us to consider a number of factors, for instance significant changes in domestic and international stocks, changes in the revenue of dairy producers in other countries or major changes in competitive costs inherent in processing.
In closing, Madam Speaker, I say to the Prime Minister, to the government, and to the Minister of Agriculture, climb out of the swimming pool and into the think tank- withdraw the recent 45 cent levy-smarten up and look further into this problem. We can compete with Europe, but to do so we must improve our strategy as world traders. We can compete with them, and can do so without forcing the dairy farmers of Canada to foot the whole bill.

speakeroldname: Mr. Leopold Corriveau (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-LEVY CHARGED ON MANUFACTURING MILK-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am forced to repeat almost the same thing I have been saying a number of times recently, because we are asked the same question all the time. Anyway, I might have an explanation for the hon. member. Producers already undertook with the Canadian government to pay export costs, under supply management programs.
One important matter remains to be clarified concerning exports. In order to do that, I will have to explain the current situation of world trade. Powdered skim milk stocks have been on the increase and prices are declining. At the beginning of 1975, skimmed milk powder was selling at 45 cents. In April, when the European Economic Community increased its exports subsidies, the price went down to 36 cents a pound. It has been declining ever since, and is now at 26 cents a pound. You must therefore understand how serious the problem is.
Faced with such a decline, Canada must choose one of two alternatives. Either we meet competition and sell at low prices, or we accumulate stocks. Clearly, the second alternative must be rejected because it would be much too costly. But we have to face the facts. If we sell at low prices, we must assume the loss because on each pound of skimmed milk powder originally priced at 64 cents, there is a loss of 37 cents. Assuming the total export volume is 200 million pounds, we get an astronomical figure of $74 million.
The government must act therefore. It must increase the export levy on industrial milk. The amount of the levy has been 90 cents a hundred weight since July 1. Although strongly criticized, such an increase is needed to maintain skimmed milk powder sales at current world prices. Let me explain. We were fully justified to announce a target price when world price was abnormal. In April, such a price still allowed to face competition, thanks to the level of levy we had then. Unfortunately, there has been since a

July 29, 1975
Adjournment Debate
radical change, and the Canadian government had no responsibility there. It is known that our department is strongly interested in exports. We have always tried to find new markets for Canadian products. The present situation leaves us with little alternative. We already examined the effects of government financing, but it would produce more problems than it would solve. Madam Speaker, I think it is relevant to say that the same question has been put to us several times. We are forced to give nearly always the same answer.

ENERGY-NATURAL GAS-POSSIBILITY OF GOVERNMENT PROMOTING POLAR PIPELINE THROUGH MANITOBA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the subject I wish to debate in this evening's adjournment debate is the critical situation facing Canada and the United States, the serious shortage of natural gas, and why the polar gas pipeline ought to be routed through Manitoba.
As you know, Madam Speaker, I and my colleagues raised this matter previously in this House. Two circumstances prompted me to raise the matter again on this occasion. The first of these is the government's inaction in attempting to find a solution to our country's impending shortage of natural gas, a shortage which will be made more serious by the expected shortages and higher prices of other forms of energy.
As an authority, may I quote the words of Mr. Bruce Wilson, former president of Union Gas of Chatham, Ontario. Speaking in Ottawa last May, Mr. Wilson said:
Reserves of natural gas are declining in Canada. There has not been a major discovery in the southern half of the western Canada sedimentary basin in the last seven years. At the same time, production rates have increased.
He summed it up by saying, "My main point is that there is a tremendous supply problem facing Canada." I hope that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) realizes this. His actions to date do not support this hope to any great extent.
The obvious course of action for the government is clear. It should take definitive action to encourage the building of a natural gas pipeline from the Arctic islands, where the reserves of the future lie. Apparently, the government has been playing around with the decision on whether to support the plans to build the Mackenzie Valley pipeline or the plans of the polar gas consortium. I believe the right decision is obvious if benefit to Canada as a whole is the main criterion.
Let me read part of an article carried in today's Ottawa Journal. The caption over the headline reads "18 Design Faults Charged." The headline is, "Pipeline Inadequate", and the body of the article, which was written in Washington reads in part as follows:
... Design on the proposed Canada-U.S. arctic natural gas pipeline is inadequate, the U.S. interior's department stated Monday.
The project which includes the Mackenzie Valley pipeline in Canada was analyzed in a 19 volume draft environment impact statement weighing 51-pounds and released by the U.S. government here.
This study listed 18 faults in the pipeline design.

... the problems involve sections of the pipeline system which would be buried in the Arctic and sub-Arctic reaches of Alaska and northern Canada.
Let me point out that Manitoba faces a serious shortage of natural gas. New homes and businesses must find alternative fuels to supply heat and power.
Two alternative routes have been suggested for this pipeline. One route would put it through eastern Keewatin and Manitoba; the other, across Hudson Strait and down through northern Quebec. May I list my reasons for thinking the Manitoba route is the cheapest and most logical alternative. Consider the matter of construction. The Manitoba route would be an all-land route, while the Quebec route would involve the spanning of a large body of water, Hudson Strait. The building of pipelines on land involves, of course, a well understood and much practised technology; building under water does not involve any well understood technology. Surely problems would arise in connection with the under water route.
Let us also consider construction aids. In this regard the Manitoba route is far ahead of the Quebec route. The main aid to construction would be the Hudson Bay railway, which would run parallel to the pipeline from Churchill to The Pas for 510 miles. That route would provide the builders of the pipeline with cheap transportation help. The very presence of a railway and highway means that supplies could be transported quickly and cheaply to construction areas.
In the first phase of construction, materials would be taken to Churchill and loaded on supply boats, which would deliver materials to points along the Hudson Bay coast where construction would be taking place. In the later phases of construction, materials would simply be unloaded along the railway and highway, at the point where construction had proceeded. As a sideline, this would provide a much needed shot in the arm for the port of Churchill and the railway.
It must also be remembered that Quebec has no such rail or road system, and one would have to be built before construction could begin. This would greatly add to the cost of building the pipeline through Quebec.
A second construction aid available in Manitoba and not in Quebec is labour. In northern Manitoba skilled construction workers may be found along the route of the pipeline, with experience in building mines, smelters, hydro developments, forestry complexes, etc., while in Quebec no such labour supply exists, simply because of lack of population.
Thus, costs of transporting labour to the construction site would be cheaper in Manitoba than Quebec. Also it must be remembered that a pipeline through Manitoba would do much to alleviate chronic unemployment problems in the area, especially among the large native population. Again it must be emphasized that while Quebec may have the same problem, it is on a lesser scale because of the smaller total population in its northern areas.
As to the area served, here again Manitoba has the edge. A pipeline through Quebec would begin to serve its use when it reached an area only about 100 miles north of Montreal; before this it would travel through 1,000 miles of sparsely populated area.
July 29, 1975

In Manitoba its benefits would be felt, with the construction of several branch lines, as far north as Baker Lake, Chesterfield, Rankin Inlet and Whalecove, and thence to the great seaport of Churchill.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, even though the hon. member did not finish his speech I believe I got the main drift of his remarks. He has suggested that the polar gas route is an immediate alternative means of supplying frontier gas. At the present time the supply from the Arctic Islands is insufficient to justify the construction of a polar route-only about 14 trillion cubic feet have been established, whereas the minimum threshold volume is estimated to be at least 20 trillion cubic feet before such a pipeline is feasible. Estimates of the volume needed could rise if unexpected costs arise in the course of
Adjournment Debate
pipeline construction or if there are physical obstructions discovered which would make the route more expensive than presently evisaged.
There is also a great deal of research development and planning work to be carried out before a polar gas pipeline can go ahead. The federal government is interested in seeing this research work carried out so that the pipeline may go forward. Possibly Petro-Can could be the vehicle for federal government participation since one of the objectives of the corporation is energy research and development.
As the minister said in the House, the government does have an interest in this pipeline because it is a 45 per cent shareholder in Panarctic. Thus, as reserves of gas are proven in the Arctic islands and the necessary technology is developed, it would become possible to go ahead with this route to deliver the gas from the Arctic regions to southern Canada.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 11.13 p.m.

Wednesday, July 30, 1975
